div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

CASE AT THE COUNTY COURT. Before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes at the Warrington County Court last Thursday, a claim was heard in:which Mr. Bonner, of Foe-street, Warrington, sought to recover £3 5s ed damages, for the loss of 30 fowls, from Mr. Alexander Clare, milkseller, living in the same district.—Mr. Dootson represented the plaintiff and Mr. Browne defended. In stating the case Mr. Dooteon observed that the plaintiffs claim was for damages for the destruction of his fowls on various dates. The claim was only a email one, but it represented thirty fowls. The plaintiff had obtained perm:ssion to allow his fowls to run on a vacant piece of land near his house in Fox-street, and at the far end of the land there was a stable rented by the defen- dant. He believed the plaintiff's bens had been trespassing on the defendant's manure heap, but the amount of damage was another question. The defendant did net like the hens on the manure heap and had spoken to the plaintiff about it. Some time in April the plaintiff found that some of his fcwls had died from poison. He spoke to the defendant about it but nothing transpired until the receipt of a letter on the let day of May from the defendant, stating that if after the Bth of May he found any of the fowle destroy- ing the manure he should not be responsible for any harm that might come to rude fowls. He (Mr. Doetson) would produce evidence showing that the defendant had threatened to kill the plaintiff's fowls. Between June and July the plaintiff lost 30 hens all of which had been poisoned. The plaintiff had been seen to place bread coated over with pbospherous on the manure heap. The fowls had gone there and afterwards died in dreadful agony. It had been painful to see the fowls die in the way they had. One was taken to a 'veterinary surgeon and he would prove that the fowl died from peisoning. Mr. Browne: They were trespassing on our property. His Honour: I don't think that justifies you is killing he fowls. The plaintiff said he lived in Fex-street and near the land his fowls used was a manure heap owned by the defendant. He complained to the defendant about throwing at his (plaintiff's)fowls whereupon the defend- ant threatened to "slur him into the brook." Witness's wife told defendant that she thought he had done enough by poisoning some fowls. The defendant replied " I will do more than that ; I will kill them all before I have finished." He had lost 30 fowls altogether between June 23rd and July lltb,and he valued them at £3 5s ed. —Crose-examined : He was aware that there was a chemical heap near his house and that Senkey Brook was close to: The plaintiff's wife stated that she visited the manure heap and saw a piece of pcisoned bread there. She took it away and she now produced it in Court. About a week after she picked up a second piece of bread from the manure heap. This wes taken to the veterinary surgeon for examination. Her daughter also picked up a pieee of bread.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne: The poison on the bread was of ea greenish colour, and she believed it to be rat poison. Clarissa Potter, Fox-street, a neighbour, stated that the defendanttold her the plaiiriff's fowls were a nuis- ance. He also added that he %you'd "stop their pick- lag." Mrs. Mclliveine, a widow, stated that she saw seven of the fowls die. Their combs were bltck. Martha Elizabeth Holloway, a chid nine years of age, said she saw the defendant going to his stable and put a piece of bread on the manure heap. She picked up the bread, smelled at it and found it dirty- It was covered with green etuff. She put it down again and went far Lily Bonner who went for it and took it to her mother.—ln answer to his Honour, witness admitted that Mr. Johesen had been questioning her as to her evidenee that day. Lilian Bonner, daughter of the plaintiff, stated that on a Friday in July trap previous witness showed her a piece of bread on the manure heap and told her to smell at it. It was a bluish green. She had heard the del en- ant say " I will kill them all when I go past." This was on the night before Walking Day.—Cress-examined, witness contradicted herself and stated that it was be- fore Walking Day when the girl showed her the piece of -breed. Benjamin Johnson, 79,F0x-street, a chair maker,stated that he had had a long experience in fowl keeping. He saw the plaintiff's fowls die, and their death was due to poisonine.—Crose examined he denied that he had been getting up plaintiff's MP. Mr. Richardson. veterinary surgeon, at Warrington, said that on July 11th Mr. Johnson b.ouelet him a piece of bread with a greenish paste on it. Is had a very strong smell of pholphercua A foal was also brought to him, and on epening it ih were strong fumes of phospherous. The death of the bird was due to eating pheepherine vermin paste. Mr. Arthur Browne said he did not know wbether his Honour considered there was a sufficient rase to answer. There was only one fowl actually proved to have died Isom poisoning. His Honour thought there was a case. Mr. Browns said Mr. Clare had been greatly annoyed by the plaintiff's hens, and they had done him infinite damage. He used to be very friendly with the plaintiff and he would swear that he had never had any such stuff as that now produced in his possession. All the poison Mr Clare had ever had was rat cheese, which was of a yellowish tint. This was put down in the stable for the purpose of killing rats. He submitted that Mr Clare was not liable for any damages. His Honour: It is quite enough to prove that he put it down. Mr. Browne proceeded to state that the defendant came to him in May for advice with reference to these hens and be told him what steps to take. Was it likely that Mr Clare would disregard what was told him and wilfully poison these hens ? Referring to the evidence of the girl Holloway Mr. Browne said it was evident that Johnson bad been telling her somohing. It was Mr. Johnson who took the fowl to the veterinary surgeon and It was he who had done mott of the work in the case. It was quite possible that these fowls had been drinking at the brook and thus got poisoned. A man named Arnold had lout six bens in the same neighbourhood and they could not have been to the defendant's place. His Honour If you could show that there was phosphorous in the chemical heap or the brook it would be a strong point. Mr. Browne said his client could not afford to pay for as analyst. The defendant was then called and said he lived at 38, Percy-street. He had never bad any phospherine 'terrain paste in his possession. He had never placed any poison anywhere outshle his stable. Be bad laid raticheese in his stable to poison rats but fowl could not get at it. He denied that he had put a piece of bread on the rcanure heap in June and July. He saw eight or ten fowls at the brook that morning. He could not say that he had seen any drinking in June or July at the brook but he bad seen them there. This was all the evidence offered. His Honour said the charge was of an exceedingly cruel and wanton nature and such as mis,tht well have bees dealt with by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to'Animals!and would have been severely brought home to defendant. He had not to administer that Act of Parliament but he had to say wi,ether the evidence satisfied him that the defendant had poisoned these fowls. If be was to believe the evidence of Clarissa Potter and Mrs. Bonner the defendant threatened to do so. The only witness called to prove that the defendant actually laid down the poison was an innocent little child who if she had hem left alone would have had great weight with him in giving his decision. He did not know that she intended to say what was untrue but it was quite clear that elle had been tutored by Johnson. The other girl contredicted herself as to the date. The evidence should bo above euspizion and he could net say that it was in this case. It was not sufficiently trust- worthy to give judgment against the defendant for destroying the fowls in this very cruel, torturing way. Be would give judgment for the defendant without Moats.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MY DEAR NELLIE, As I have told you before, the fashions in nead- gear remains unchanged. Hats are chiefly of the sailor order with a peak over the forehead, but I hardly think they are becoming on the whole. So long as the hat is small, and not over-trimmed, nor perishable, any kind really is admissible. Very pretty sailors are being turned out trimmed with crepe de chine scarves, the fringed ends hanging over the brim at one side, with a quill thrust through the scarf in front; one side is lifted off the head, by a chou of ribbon or a couple of roses. Doubtless for morning wear many of the new bems capelines will be seen about, being :ight, pretty, and suitable. They have pleated muslin brims, with straw jam-pot crowns and large bows, and are eminently becnming to young, fresh faces. Toque g made entirely of straw, crinkled up into all sorts of fantastic shapes, with a large straw bow in frout, are preferred by those to whom the sailor is not becoming, and there is nothing in them to spoil, either with sun or wet. Fancy hats retain their former style of trimming, viz., with feathers, flowers and laces.

Children are not forg-itten this hot weather. And oe;thor Fh.luld they be. I think it is mar- velluu-i the d:staz,e!, some of them cover in the coo re of a day. Bat sometimes they must present a smart appearance. White seems the all- fa4iion now, and I ihink rightly so. I sal, a child the other day with a very sensible dress on. It was low in the throat and over the shoulders fell a very small cape of lace. The sleeves of the dress wore loose, and on the fore- arm were tied up with ribbons. A very pretty white sash completed the dress.

I saw a very nice dress at a fashionable race course recently, and although it was a black one it really looked very cool. It was a black chiffon striped longitudinally, and lined with white chiffon, and had a bodice of the lace, vttry light, and open in design, with a narrow black velvet belt, and a band of black velvet up the front, sewn with diamond buttons. The dress was cut away at the throat, to show the usual strip of pearls, now bScome almost an indispensable adjunct of a smart costume, and also a necklace of turquoises and diamonds, for the wearing of coloured jewels in the daytime has become quite fashionable.

From my observations lately I rather fancy that dark blue serge finds more wearers than red. For either, however, might be recommended that style with triple collars of white drill ; plainly machine-stitched skirt and sleeves ; buttons bear- ing might fasten the bodice down bv the side, and the necktie could well be of black. The black neck- tie, by the way, is much in favour this year, and shares attention with the tie of spotted surah. Talking of spotted neckties reminds me of the latest novelty in ties, made in white muslin, spotted all over with red, white, or blue, and bearing plain stitched hems. These look very well with serge gowns, and I have also seen one of them most successfully used to trim a plain sailor hat. Another way of trimming a sailor hat no less successfully is with a fringed scarf of pale blue crepe de chine, the front of the crown being pierced with a single quill. Let me caution you against succumbing to any particular colour that may happen to be the rage. Neutral tints are safest, for they do not " date " themselves, and they wear beat. Navy blue is both becoming and serviceable, and so, too, is brown, and either might be chosen for the tailor- made. For the dressy toilet something near these tones ought to be chosen, they can easily be brightened with a little good lace, say as yoke and collar. Several gowns are being turned out with long lace or net sleeves coming right down on to the hand, as far as the knuckles, shaped like a mitten, with a thumb piece—these are cool, tight gloves, which we one and all abhor this weather, and allow of a display of rings, which, by the way, are immensely worn now, as many as the fingers can carry, and as large as good taste permits. I think that one of the most successful gowns I have seen of late was of beautifully fine white cloth, cut with a short open coat rounded off from the fronts, and lined with white satin, with a collar and novel-shaped revers embroidered over with gold braid, and worn over a skirt of white satin. The skirt had a pointed panel let in on the left side closely braided with gold as the revers. Your loving JENNIE.

"WOMEN'S CHAT."

The departure of the Duchess of Albany on a three years' visit to ;Germany, is a matter of considerable re- gret to her very large circle of friends, and the same may be said of the Princess Alice, who in her manner and ways, so closely resembles her mother. But ti e youthful heir-apparent to the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg- Gotha, is not so great a favourite. Until lately he has always shewn himself as a somewhat morbid, unsociable boy, andynow,his position in life is so vastly improved, he is so elated as to lose sight of tact altogether. The Duchess of Altany was never a great favcurite with the Queen, and when some years after the death of the Duke, she asked permission to marry a leaaing statesman, and was refused, affairs became very strained between Her Majesty and the widow of her youngelt son. The Queen has always insisted on mourning being worn by the Duchess, and it is whispered that the hall- mourning colours lately donned by Her Royal Highness, have given further serious offence to the Sovereign.. Altogether the Duchess of Albany can scarcely have been sorry to leave this country, in which she has suffered so many slights, and restrictions. There are great rejoicings in the North this month, in honour of Lady Cromertie, who attains her majority, , and succeeds to the large family estates. The young Countess is the inheritrix in the female line of the 'famous Scottish family of Hay-MacKenzie, formerly , Earls of Cromartie in the Peerage of Scotland. Four I years ago she was created, by Her Majesty, a Peeress in her own right. It is two years since she made her debut in London scciety,chaperoned by the Ducheq; of Suther- land who is much attached to her young kinswoman.. The other young Scotch millionaire is Lady Mary , Hamilton. The only daughter of the late Duke, she was left, at toe age of ten, the whole of his unentailed estates and property, and at the age of twenty-one, she will become absolute mistress of a property bringing in considerably over £lOO,OOO a year. The richest un- married woman we have among us at the present time however, is an American—Miss May. Goelet. At the age of twenty-five the will become the possessor of the enor- mous total of ten million pounds ,and be one of the great- est. ground landlords of New York. Satin has at length lost favour for bridal gowns. At one time it was the regulation fabric, and any other was regarded as out of place and cut of Vogue. But we have changed all that, and now crepe de chine, lace, mousseline, and chiffon robes obtain, and very fascinat- ing they are, especially when worn by youthful pretty brides. Many and various have been the devices of late arranged to take the place of the shower bouquet, but none have really " caught on," and the shower bouquet, than which nothing is more charming and be- coming, once again holds a foremost place in our affec- tions.

Lady Arabella Romilly, and Miss Evelyn Lang have lately been respectively deprecating and defending long engagements, in the columns of a woman's paper. It is a little difficult to see how any Procrustean rule can be made on this subject. Montaigne, had his opinion been asked, would have said that it did not matter whether the parties were married at the end of a long or short engagement, in either case they would have occasion for regret. The majority of people will probably say that it depends upon circumstances, and that in such mat- ters it is not much use to make rules for other people, upon whom they will have no influence. The persons most concerned will continue to consult the!r own con- venience and interests, or still more likely their inclina- tions, and it is to be feared that some of them may be rude enough to say that they do not see what business it is of anybody else. In Berlin the servant girls have taken advantage of the holiday season to organise a special Congress for the ventilation of their grievances. They want more holi- days, higher wages, and greater liberty, but the most important pointit seems is concerned with the question of followers—and the agitation is chiefly directed against their prohibition. Such troubles are not of course confined to any one country—they extend all over the world—but in Germany they have now assumed a political importance, and the Socialists have naturally taken up the cause of the housemaid and her followers. No doubt we shall soon have similar developments on this side of the German Ocean.

A London householder recently advertiEed for others to join him in importing Chinese servants. Such a remedy for the everlasting trouble with servants has often been discussed, but it is not practicable. Native servants are all very well in the East, where their employers never concern themselves with what they are doing when off duty, which means the greater part of every day. They are happy and contented in their own surroundings, and very little in fact is expected of them. Ten or a dozen servants are the usual thing in quite small and modern establishments, and betwcen them they divide the work, which would be done over here by a cook and housemaid, and even then house-cleaning is usually regarded as unnecessary and superfluous. Good Chinese servants may be found anywhere in the Far East, but in this country they would be out of their element, and would quickly prove a greater nuisance than those troubles which are more familiar to us.

Black picture hats are enjoying a wide vogue, and highly becoming they prove to the majority. This is probably due to the fact that the black hat has a toning down effect, so desirable just down, when the gayest of gay toilettes are wore in the day time. However "ball- like" the gown may be, one's appearance can almost always be saved from vulgarity by crowning oneself with a black hat, and adding a touch of black to the neck and waist, and donning black shoes and stockings. With regard to the colours likely to be best worn this coming autumn, leaver brown bids fair to enjoy a foremost place. This is a very becoming tint to some. but on the other band there are numbers of complexions that should never be seen near it. For these latter, however, there is still hope in the world fashionable,for blue promises to hold its own well, also grey. The old-fashioned game of cropret is in great favour this summer, and few country gardens there are that

boast not a lawn, set aside for this particular pastime. It is though a mach more difficult game than it used to be. Every year some new test is added to the—appar- ently—simple task of getting through the iron hoops. FISH ScALLors.—Take any cooked fish, divide into flakes, place in china shells with some melt?Ai butter, or shrimp sauce. Add a little chopped parsley, pepper, and salt, and cover with brown crumbs and a few picces of butter, and bake until quite hot. , " MADGE."

div.head: WEST AUSTRALIAN SHARES.
div.p: WEST AUSTRALIAN SHARES.
HANNAN'S ASSOCIATED MINES.

We referred recently to the £1 fully-paid shares cf Hannan's Associated Mines (Limited) as well worth the attention of the speculativer investor at their then price of 10e. per share. Since then they have been largely dealt in on the London Stock Exchange, and are now quoted at about 15a. Mr. W. G. Brookman, the die- ccverer of the Grrat Boulder and other successful West Australian Mines, states in his report as follows " You have an extremely valuable combination of leases,which will, I have no doubt, prove to contain the Great Boulder Main Lodes,the Ivanhoe Main Lodes,and others, and probably the Lake View Lode. I congratulate you on securing it, and I have no hesitation in recommend- ing this property as one which will yield handsome divi- dends." Bannan's AFsociated Mines (Limited) owe' eleven mining leases, with an area of about two hundred and twenty-eiOrt acres,situated on the famous Hannan'e Field,Kalgoorlie,only one hundred and sixty chains south of the Greht Boulder,Lake View, and Ivanhoe Mines,and it is expected that the company will strike the celebrated Ivanhoe Lode at the 500 it. level, in which case the price of the shares 'sill rise out of all proportion to pre- sent quotations.

div.head: BANKRUPTCY OF WARRINGTON
div.p: BANKRUPTCY OF WARRINGTON
BUT,I,DEII S.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court on Friday before Mr. tiegistrar Ridgway two local builders were examined with respect to their bankruptcy. The first case was that of Herbert Bowling Ezard, residing and carrying on business as a joiner and builder at Victoria-road, Poulton-with-Fearnhead. The liabilities are expected to rank at £3849 19s 4d The assets are stated and estimated by the bank- rupt to produce £2046 16s 3d, leaving a deficiency of £lBO3 3s Id. In his statement at the Official Receiver's Office, the bankrupt alleged as the causes of failure" Want of capital, over building, failure to obtain further advances, loss of rent through want of tenants, heavy expenses of filling up land at Ellesmere Port and heavy law costs." The bankrupt stated that he commenced business in February. 1895 with £5O his savings. He has kept a ca,h book containing all his receipts and payments during the whole period he carried on business, but which has never been added up or balanced. The securities in the hands of creoitors fully or partly secured are first and second charges on 11 houses, 2 villas, and 1 shop in Victoria-road, Fearnhead ; 1 house in Yearnhead-lane, Padget e ; 10 houses numbers 83 to 101 in Marsh House-lane; 11 houses, numbers 35 to 43 and 47 to 57, in Willis-street : 17 houses in Victoria-road and Lingdale Avenue, Fearnhead ; 24 houses in Liverpool-road, Sankey; 16 (incomplete) houses in Huntley-street, Sankey; and 37 (incom- plete) houses in Ezard-street, Ellesmere Port. —The Assistant Official Receiver said he did not propose to take the public examination that day because the main questions turned almost entirely ' on accounts. He would ask the Registrar to make an order for the debtor to file a cash 'account for the full period of his trading.—The debtor said he thought he would be able to supply what was needed.—The Registrar made an order for the ac- count to be filed within fourteen days and ad- journed the public examination of the debtor to Friday, September Ist at 2 o'clock. James Astley, residing at 123, Orford-lane, and carrying on business as a builder at Long-lane, Longford, then appeared for his public examination in bankruptcy. The cause of failure as alleged by the bankrupt was "The building of pro- perty on an insanitary site." He stated that he commenced business at Long-lane at in September last, without capital, but was receiv- inv royalties in respect. of patent for an oven. The unsecured liabilities of £256 us lid were for loans £4O 18s; goods sold and delivered £213 us 10d; professional charges -ST 2s. The securities held by creditors fully secured were a mortgage on five leasehold houses in Long-lane,and a mortgage on 8 leasehold houses (in course of erection) in the same lane and held by a creditor partly secured.—The examination of the debtor, who was stone deaf,was closed.

REVENGE OF VALERIE:
A ROMANCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA.
BY HUME NISBET,
Author of "A Sweet Sinner," "Bail Up," "The Rebel Chief," "Kings of the Sea," "Hunting for Gold, "The Swampers," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Sir Lewis Eastlake, twenty-four years of age, is introduced to the reader, as he is "going the pace," at a London gambling club. There, in company with a friend. Captain Eric St. Arnoul, he gets into an altercation, which results in a duel, at Cherbourg. His opponent is killed in this. He has a strong sentimental friendship with the Duchess of Valerie, at Genoa,a widow lady, in the prime of her beauty, who, in affection for him, backs the financier, who lends him money. Captain St. Arnoul, his com- panion, who is a cousin of the Duchess, informs her that Sir Lewis had:been injured in the duel, and, in view of the other man's death, it is thought prudent he should be removed from Cherbourg. The Duchess hears that he is in charge of a Cherbourg doctor, who is an old friend, and his sister, who is a nurse. She fears that he may be arrested, and arranges with the Captain for him to be taken by the nurse to her seat at Falaise, and she follows on afterwards. The Duchess finds, to her regret, on her arrival at Falaise, that the nurse "Hope " is young and good-looking, and a friend of Sir Lewis from childhood. After Hope has left he tells the Duchess that he and Hope had been engaged for years, and that before the duel they were married privately. Sir Lewis Eastlake goes out to Klondike. and is followed by a man who calls himself Bill Sykes, and appears to be acting under instructions.
CHAPTER IX. HOPE EASTLAKE BEGINS HER TROUBLES. Twelve months had passed since Hope Eastlake had parted with her husband, and now she was in London, with an infant to look after and not a

friend to help her. Twelve months since they Parted, after that sweet honeymoon at Falaise, the only memory now for her aching heart to live upon. Twelve months since his lips last touched hers, and eleven months since the last of his letters had been received. He had written from New York, Vancouver and Dyea ; affectionate and cheerful letters. Then had come that long and awful blank. He was going over the Chilkoot Pass; and it seemed as if that cruel Pass had swallowed him up, leaving no trace to point to his fate. He had gone out of her life with a gay farewell, leaving her a bitter legacy of

sorrow,-aiixiety and trouble-. _ _ While they were together all seemed to point to happine3s, peace and prosperity. The Duchess Valerie was their friend undoubtedly, for had she not placed the Chateau of Falaise, with all its comforts, at their free disposal? What a dream of bliss those few bright months had been, when she _ _ _
had Lewis all to heraelf. Only one cloud then lay upon the horizon of that paradise—the thought of her adored husband's departure. But even that

seemed to be a small Cloud with the prospects before them. "The Klondike Moose Mining Com- pany," of which he was a director, was a large and flourishing concern. He had been sent out, with a free hand, to investigate the claims already pur- chased and negotiate for others. His individual shares in all future purchases were to be a quarter profit, and on all that he discovered himself, half. Mr. Stephen Belwood had come over and ad-. vanced the money required on the security of her good brother's name. It was a six months' bill, but the money-lender had promised to renew it, as required, to suit the convenience of the borrower and his backer.
Her brother signed the bill willingly enough, for, after her, he loved no one so much in the world as her husband. Sir Lewis made over his life policy,

after paying out of the loans the premium for the next year; a heavy one it was, under the circum- stances, before the company would tae the risk. But that had been settled at last, and the amount insured more than trebled what had been borrowed.

Her brother also had money invested in what was considered a safe thing, so that there did not seem any great danger in obliging his friend and brother sr, this momentous crisis of their lives. Until the departure of her husband only that little cloud of sorrow of parting lay in their love- sky. But he had not been gone a week before other clouds began to surge up. First it was the fatal duel, which the friends of the dead young man raked up. Ugly rumours were spread about, that it had been unfairly fought, and, what was more serious to her brother's reputation,

that he had either wilfully or ignorantly mis- managed the wounded patient. He tried to refute those vague charges by appeal- ing to the French surgeon who had attended with him the death-bed of the unfortunate Charles Bingham; but although this rival did not openly accuse him, he did worse, for he did not defend him. Another case ended fatally, and again the evil report went about that he had mismanaged it; and after this his brother-practitioners refused to meet him in consultation. By great care and at considerable expense he had built up a good practice for himself at Cherbourg, and in less than a month he found himself with hardly a patient. The wealthy had employed him before; now only a few of the poor and feeless patients were left, so fragile is the reputation of a professional man. Dr. Walth•ed was by no means a strong man. Although he kept the matter a secret, he had suffered from heart disease for some years, and these troubles preyed upon his sensitive mind terribly. He tried to be calm for the sake of his sister, but he never went out now without a restorative. At this time one of his poor patients died of malignant puerperal fever, and that ended his career as a doctor at Cherbourg. He dared not attend another case, for only a complete change of scene would remove the danger of infection from him. He, therefore, sold his practice at about fifty times less than he had paid for it, and prepared to leave Cherbourg. Then the last blow fell upon him, which killed him as swiftly as a stroke of lightning could have done. He had written to withdraw his money from where it was invested, and while wait- ing on a reply the crushing tidings came that one of the principals had absconded and left affairs in a state of utter bankruptcy. He was ruined now, for that bill was almost due. He rose from the breakfast-table after reading the awful news, to go to his study. But he never reached the door, for half-way across the room he suddenly reeled and sank upon the carpet. Hope Eastlake had lost her brother and only protector. An evil destiny seemed to be hunting the poor young wife relentlessly. She had borne the separation from her husband bravely, and striven her hardest to comfort her brother under these strokes of adversity. Now, in this sudden and unexpected bereavement, Fate seemed to have emptied its quiver upon her. Ah, if she could have read the future, how little all this would have seemed for a human heart to endure! She had made no friends in France, at least no real friends. We are all one family as the descendants of the first pair, yet whereas Englishmen may pity and succour the refugee foreigner, Frerrchmen and Germans, when they shew pity at all, to the penniless outcast, have only pity and sympathy for their own countrymen. The foreigner is promptly kicked out of these lands as soon as misfortune comes upon him and he has spent his money. They have no space nor charity for outside paupers. That is the duty of "per- fidious" Albion, the contemptible weakness of broad-backed, soft-hearted, wooden-headed Johnny Bull.

Her dead brother had been a rival of Monsieur Crapaud on his native soil, which made the offence greater to those democrats. They don't think it at all unfair to provide Jon Bull with doctors, dentists, hairdressers, costumiers, authors, and painters, because he is simple enough to admire foreign produce and prefer it to his own. But they are not so soft. They will not tolerate anything literary, artistic or scientific outside their own compatriots. They are patriotic and national. What was this afflicted lady to do? Where turn for help or consolation? The people who had invited her to their "At Homes" while her brother was prosperous had turned their backs upon her at the first puff of the adverse gales. There was little time left Hope to lament over the brother she had lost. We may sit down and mourn Over our dead when kind friends are round us to take the sordid details out of our sight and hearing. No kind friends were near to Hope East- lake, therefore she had to brace up and face the trouble by herself. Had she any friends in England, since she had none in Cherbourg? No; she could not recollect any, only her absent husband, and his mother, who had died five years before. Her brother had led a retired life in England. and their uarents had died while she was still a cilia; as for other relations, she did not know anything about them,

She was absolutely alone in the world, as tar as dhe knew. Alone, and expecting to be a mother in a few months. Two nights she sat by the bier of her dead brother, lookinf, at his intellectual and death-beautified face, and thinking out the problem of life and death. As Hamlet thought it out; as so many countless martyrs to life have thought it out. Like Hamlet, to rise wearied but hopeless of the issue. "To be, or not to be ? " When men sit down to reason this gloomy philosophy to its bitter end, it all depends upon their madness how the logic terminates. When women in the condition of Hope Eastlake sit down to reason out this question, there can only be one decision, and that is the decision of the most implacable laws. "I must wait, bear all things, suffer all things, for this precious gift of God, which must be ushered into earth." No wife, who believed in her husband, ever was a traitress to her sacred charge, since the human family commenced. Hope rose from her self-communings, and with fervent prayers to Heaven braced herself up for her coming duty and her holy gift. She had money enough to bury her brother and pay for the atten- tions of those hirelings who came about her at this time; then with the lawyer she went through his papers. Dr. Waldred had insured his life for four thousand pounds, and left this, with his other personal effects, to her. These personal effects when they were sold brought in fifty pounds. He had a little over three hundred pounds in the bank at the time of his decease. But the bill which the money-lender held over her absent husband and her dead brother was for five thousand pounds. On the morning after the funeral, Mr. Stephen Belwood appeared before her, and presenting it, asked for a settlement. It was not due for another fortnight, but she did not know about these legalities. Mr. Stephen Belwood was rather a melancholy, white-faced man of about thirty-five. He was well dressed, with the orthodox moustache, and a gentlemanly-looking fellow, so long as he did not open his mouth. When he did, he exhibited decided traces of a defective education. Yet he was deferential all through the interview. He put it before her that he was not the principal in the 'money-lending business, but only a manager looking after other people's money. He had exceeded privileges in doing the business at all, out of friendship and kindness to her absent husband. Now, if she left him in the lurch, he would be a ruined man. This appeal of Mr. Stephen Belwood touched Hope, as he expected it would. She had to own that he had been affable and kind on his last visit to Falaise, whilst the borrowing was being nego- tiated, also that he was only asking his rights now, and asking it in a very humble and deprecating way. She was alone and friendless in a. foreign land, and this man was a countryman—he was, so far as his own birth was concerned, but he belonged to the tribe of Israel, who are aliens in every country, for all that. She gave him her confidence, and he was most sympathetic. She promised to give him the four thousand pounds from the insurance and the three hundred pounds from the bank. But when he heard that she would have only fifty pounds left he became chivalrous. He said that he would be satisfied meanwhile with four thousand two hundred and fifty, leaving her a clear hundred to begin the world with. "Hit will take you to London, Lady Eastlake," he said respectfully, "hand hif you will permit me to be your hescort I shall get you comfortable lodgings with ha friend of mine while you look about.' He dropped his h's and picked them up at the most unexpected places, but he was a polite and respectful man, and as she looked at his serious face and filmy dark eyes she had no fear of him. He was a delicate-looking man, narrow-chested, red-lipped, and with a nervous cough. "I have had some experience in nursing, and I'd like to be a nurse," .she said, after they had finished their business conversation. "Yes. I think hi can be hof use to you 'ere also, if you will make me your agent in London. I 'ave a good number of clients who will be 'appy to , hoblige me in this matter." Poor Hope—Lady Eastlake—was grateful for his kindly aid. He stayed in Cherbourg until she had settled all her business, then he escorted her in the most chivalrous manner across the Channel and provided her with modest lodgings in London, out in the Brixton direction.
CHAPTER X. HOPE EASTLAKE AT BRIXTON.

Hope Eastlake departed from Cherbourg without saying good-bye to those fair-weather friends, and left behind her in consequence a goodly number of active evil-wishers. She went quite openly away with the money-lender, and permitted him to attend upon her en route, feeling grateful to him for his attentions. She did not dream that misconstruc- tion could be put upon this action of hers, for Mr. Stephen Belwood never, by the slightest look or word, offended her susceptibility. He wasn't exactly the man she would have chosen for a friend at any time, had she been given any choice in the matter. He was by no means an entertaining companion, as there was only one subject he could speak upon, and this subject wasn't one that interested her at all—money and the quickest methods of making it. True, she wanted to make enough to keep her respectably, but that modest ambition was not, in Mr. Stephen Belwood's inind, worth considera- tion.

Literature, with the exception of the Exchange and Stock Market literature, was totally a terra incognita to Mr. Stephen Belwood. He had never read a verse of poetry in his life. As for art—well, at times he dealt with old masters to his groaning clients, but he never spoke about these masterpieces outside business hours, and as he knew nothing. about other art or artists, he could not be drawn in these directions. Science was not at all in his line, except the science of assaying. He knew that branch pretty well as far as the testing of gold and silver was concerned. _ _

He knew, however, the state of the City pulse to a beat, and Was an expert at rises and falls of stock, but as this knowledge did not appear to interest Hope he discreetly held his tongue. This was a virtue which Mr. Stephen Belwood had, if he had few others. He seldom gave strangers the opportunity of hearing how badly his father had treated him in the matter of education. His words were golden, and he didn't pitch about his gold recklessly. In manner he was mild, sedate, and self- depreciating—a shy, retiring and modest man, easily domesticated, one would have said who did not know his profession or himself. His eyes were filmy and dark, his nose not too pronounced, although slightly Semitic in shape. Those dim eyes, with the chalky complexion, sunken cheeks, and vivid scarlet lips, gave him the delicate and wearied appearance of a man far advanced in con- sumption, which the short painful cough seemed to confirm. He did not put on any airs of gallantry or protection towards his fellow-passenger on the passage. He bought her ticket for her, and calmly accepted the money from her when he gave it to her. He found a good seat for her on the sheltered side of the boat, gathered her mantle about her, and acted only as any well-behaved man would act under the circumstances. -

He did not intrude upon her in any way, although he kept near enough to attend to her wants. To Hope, who had not yet seen any other specimen of his tribe, Stephen Belwood could not possibly have treated her more kindly and delicately. Womanlike, she began to invest him with qualities, which, had she expressed them, would have made him grin under his hand and wonder at her imagi- nation. She thought his silence, which really chanced because he had nothing to say, was out of consideration for her recent bereavement, and respected him for that fancied delicacy. His habitually-wearied and sad-looking visage appeared to her caused by his sincere sympathy. She even honoured him for accepting her passage money and allowing her to pay the steward for her refresh- ments. These were the actions of a man who did not wish a comparative stranger, as she was to him, to feel herself placed under any pecuniary obliga- tion to him. She even went further in her good quality creating, for she began to feel that, although a money-lender and company promoter, he must have a disinterested desire to befriend her as far as he could, out of sympathy for her lonely position and for the sake of her absent husband. Not being a very deep reader of character, she could not know that this sad-faced, shy man was acting according to instructions in now taking her away from France; that she was being made the unconscious victim of as vile, shameful and cowardly a plot as ever revengeful woman concocted, and loathsome parasite carried out—to bring a stain upon a fair and spotless reputation. She had no means of knowing that her brother had been hounded to death by the same secret-enemy and her agent, and that already in Cherbourg her name had h—rs•me a 'mg, ora amonqst those she had ones gnown.ishe would not have believed it at this hour, even if told, that this chalk-faced scoundrel bad made and won a bet on her innocence, that amongst thoso who last left the packet were tw

gentlemen who firmly believed that she had gone a 0 - the mistress of this money-lender. She was too ignorant of the world as yet to be able to grasp at these evil things, nor was she aware of the other reasons her modest companion had for keeping her under his watchful eyes, and allowing her no other adviser for the present. - - -

A week or two must yet pass before the insurance company would pay her claim upon them. From the reading of her brother's will Stephen Belwood was perfectly aware that, legally, he could not claim a penny from her. She had given him already the .two hundred and fifty pounds from the bank, and felt grateful, poor innocent, for the fifty which he had allowed her to retain for her own use. It appeared so like a gift that she could not be suspicious of this benefactor. She had promised to deliver over to him the four thousand when she got it, and he meant to secure that cheque before he relaxed for an instant his kindly care of her. He was terribly anxious about that four thousand pounds, and this made him pre-occupied and melancholy-looking as he hovered so devotedly near her. To prevent her from making any casual acquaintance occupied his Napoleonic mind all the passage over. This drove away both his appetite and the mal de mer from him. There is no surer preventive of sea-sickness than a mind engrossed in other matters. As for spending a shilling of his own money on his companion, such an ides never entered the businesslike thoughts of Stephert Belwood. He only expended money as fishers purchase bait. He had already baited his hook with that fifty pounds, which was considered quite sufficient outlay for his purpose. Mr. Stephen Belwood, like all true capitalists and money-spinners, looked carefully after the pence. He could spend, without a murmur, large sums on.:,expensive champagne lunches or dinners when he. had an object in view, but he gave the meanest of tips to the waiters. He did not grudge either the contributions which his private vices drew from him at times, where his vanity or ruling passions were concerned, but he would dispute his cab fare and beat the hoot-black down to the lowest fraction. What he spent was either for , ostentation or for the purposes of business. He had never in his life wasted a cent upon charity or on friendship. But Hope could not know this. Indeed, much more astute judges had been deceived in the character of Stephen Belwood. The lodgings in London, to which he recom- mended her and took her as soon as they arrived, were in one of the numerous and closely packed side streets between Camberwell and Brixton; small house of three floors, with a strip of about two feet of front garden and a back-yard of some half-. dozen paces. After the open spaces of Cherbourg, Hope felt crushed in by brick walls and overlooked by windows. The only line of sky was that above the roof, a very circumscribed patch of dingy grey. The landlady wa..„ a Jewess of about twenty-nine, fat, strong - featured, and lavishly powdered; indeed, she appeared to use powder instead of soap and water. She was a very dressy woman, how- ever, who left the duties of looking after her lodgers to her Christian, or, rather, un-christian, drab of a servant.

Her husband was a clerk in one of the establish- ments of Mr. Stephen Belwood; a little sharp-. visaged, hook-nosed Israelite of forty. Hope did not see much of her landlord, as his hours of toil were long and arduous. Mr. Stephen Belwood had wired on the arrival. of the packet at Weymouth, and Mrs. Solomon Davis had prepared one of her back rooms upstairs for her lodger. It was a small room, and meanly furnished, but the rent satisfied Hope. Five shillings a week, with the use of the kitchen range. Lights, coal and attendance extra. Hope decided that she would wait upon herself for the present, and thus she started life in London. "You 'ad better 'ave your letters haddressed to my City office," suggested Mr. Belwood. "It will save you from hany undue curiosity supposing hani letters came with your title on them. Sir Lewis Eastlake will also be easier hin his mind if he knows I am looking hafter your interests." Hope was pleased to fall in with these arrange-. meats. She had resolved to call herself Mrs. Eastlake until her husband's return. A title WBl superfluous and ridiculous amidst such surround- ings, and as a nurse it would only be a bar to her chances of engagements. "It is indeed good of you to take this interest in me, Mr. Belwood," she said gratefully to the cold- blooded reptile. "You will not forget to let me hear tidings of my husband when you get them, also, if you can, get me some work to do?" "I shan't forget. You know my haddress. When you want my hadvice, come and see me. When I 'ave hany news or business to talk about, I'll run hover and see you. I 'ope you'll be com- fortable here. Mr. Davis has been in my employ.. ment for many years, and 'as proved himself trustworthy in hevery ...respect. Has for Mrs. Davis, the different people whom I 'ave sent to her 'ave halways been satisfied with her treatment; there- fore I 'ope she will suit you. If not, let me know hat once, and I'll find hanother respectable place for you. One thing: she will not interfere with you in any way." "Oh, I shall do all right if I can get work," answered Hope wearily.. "Have patience, and that will come halso. Things look slow sometimes in London, but they are sure to those who can wait. I'll find you a for private customers, I have no donbt. By the way, as we are constantly sending out messages and stock to the Yukon, if you like to forward your letters and packages through my hands, they will cost you nothing." He spoke with his customary wearied and in- different tones. No eagerness was discernible iii his voice or face, no expectant light in his well - trained filmy eyes, yet on the answer of Hope much depended. He could not stop her letters on English or Canadian soil. At Wrangel? Perhaps; but the process would be costly, and there were decided risks attending. The purchased postal clerk mio be removed, or become romantic and scrupulous. If she delivered herself into his hands, it was so much extra expense saved and put into his own pocket. Hope Eastlake fell into the trap, and delivered herself over to the enemy for the usual mess of pottage. She felt that she must study economy every way she could, for the sake of her unbora child, and doubtless her letters and packets would go much safer through the hands of this businesil man than by ordinary postage. "You are indeed kind to propose this, and shall accept your generous offer." "Very well. Give hall you want to forward tf' your 'usband to my clerk Solomon Davis, and ~ will see that they go bout by the swiftest route." The game—the sorry game of the wolf and the, lamb—was played successfully. Stephen Belwoee rose, with a little dry cough, wiped some moisture from his pallid nose and brow on his carnbri° handkerchief, and took his departure respectfully. There was little fear about his victim now, witllA Mr. and Mrs. Davis to look after her. He b6"' them all in his clammy grip. Hope rested that day and night, and the morning she went out and laid in a stock of paPer' pens and ink. She wrote to her husband a letter of twenty-feu:, pages, revealing secrets to him which ought to made him the proudest and happiest man 'll Yukon, if he had received this epistle of love' faith and duty. div.head: W. AND I.
div.p: W. AND I.

During the late James Wyllie's first tour through America he paid a couple of visits to Hartford!Con- necticut. In the course of the second visit the chess editor of the "Hartford 'limes" had a sitting with the whilom "Herd Laddie," and, under the heading "W. and I," thus recounts his experience with the champion One day last week Mr. Brown, a member of the Hartford Chess and Checker Club, faveured us with a call. He was accompanied by a portly personage who reminds us, not exactly of the "fine ould Irish gentleman," but of a bluff, good natured Scotchman. He was introduced to us as "Mr. Wyllie, the checker champion of the world." Then it was that the checker skill, which had lain dormant in our boots since our boyhood days, when we felt that we were "some pumpkins" on a checker board, strutted forth yearning for more glory. And what an excellent chance for glory. The checker Champion of the world stood ready to give us glory or give us healthy recreation. The champion didn't look as if he could whip all creation,and we fondly reckoned that if we could get him scared he was our mutton. But how to scare him was the conun- drum. Finally we asked him if he did not consider himself the Goliath of the checker world, but his modesty prevented an answer. If we could only have got him to assume gigantic proportions, we NV ere calculating to get into David's boots and then taunt him about that little affair theßible tells about. That would have fetched him we guess.l3,eing unable to bring this about,the only thing left was to go for him with his own weapons,and vanquish the Scotch gamecock at his own game. Not having any checker men handy, we placed eight pawns, two rooks, and two bishops on the board,and Mr. Wyllie having done the same, we were ready for the affray. We had the Blacks and shoved a centre man first. The Scotchmln timidly pushed a man on the left side. " Ah, ha," we thought," yon'ra a gone coon. We can whip any man at checkers who plays a side game." We moved again, and so did he, and to all appearance the game was even. Could this be the chatnnion of the

world? We felt a glow of pride at the idea of holding the king of checkers in check. We swelled with admirattion at our prowess. Yes f two moves on a side and the go.:ne still even. If our antagonist had Rot been playing a side igame we might have been tempted to call it a draw. And as it turned out, we wish we had. At that point the game could nave been drawn—by mutual con- sent or a span ot horses ; but three or four moves later it couldn't have been drawn by a team of elephants. Reason. Wyllie moved up apiece where we could cake it. We thought it was an oversight, and magnanimously pointed out hi ~3 error. lie was too magnanimous to take it back, and left it there. Thinking we would not permit a descendant of the land of Wallace to outdo one of George Washing- ton's countrymen in a deed of generosity, we refused to take it, and shot a Bishop across the board, attacking one of Wyllie's Rooks. he champion seclerl back in his chair and gazed at us with astonishment. We felt flattered at the look. It was a tribute to genius. But our enthu.dasm was dampened a moment later when he replaced the Bishop and, pointing to the man "en prise," said "jump." Very well, we thought, if he wants ta sacrifice a min, why, we'll take it. We did so. Then he moved up another for us to take. Well, we thought, if he wants to play a game of " give away" we are his men. So we jumped again. Now it was his turn to jump, and we made him play leap frog over four of our men. As soon as he saw that we had the best of him on "give away," he settled down to cneckers ag,ain,and the change gave him the best of it. From this point to the close all we tried to do was to get a King, and we gained our object with ridiculous ease. All the champions in the world can't skunk us at checkers. If Wyllie hadn't led us into a game of "give away," we might have won that game of checkers.

A MILL GIRL'S QUEER NOTION.

A GIRL who used to w ork as a " winder " at Eastfield Mills, near Halifax, has been the subject of one of the most remarkable delusions, if we may believe an article in the " Halif ix Guardian," which gives an ac- count of the affair with the girl's name and address— Edith Wilkinson, Mill View. Lumbrook, helf (a place near Halifax). Here is her account of herself : " My mother," she said, " used to get cree!s with me for my sick fancies, and then I would calm down. I always wanted to be flying away. I felt 'funny' in some way. My mother was always win me. I got up one night, and my sister said that I stood on the stair- rail. I don't know how I got there; bat she pulled sae off and put me back to bed again. I had to sleep with my mother for twelve months, and I'd say to her, ' 06,don't fall asleep and leave me, mother ! ' I ducal% trust my- self with anyone but my mother.' "My trouble," she continued, "began with in- fluenza, and I was left with erysipelas in my face. I got weaker and weaker. and I was taken to all sorts of doctors. 'They all said I was suffering from nervous debility from head to feet. I was at home for fifteen weeks, and I could do no work. I kept to my bed for three weeks, and could not go out of doors. I had to be taken out like a baby. "At that time—four years ago new—one of ths neighbours gave me a book about Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people, and suggested that I should try them. So my brother got me a box, and I began to use them. I got one box every week for some time before I began to feel better, bat went oa with tiara un- til I was cured. Now lam working again as a winder. I tell everyone that I should have been dead but for Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. lam twenty-one years of age.

" I got my brother, Joseph Bramwell Wilkinson, to take them. He felt the same as I did when I was ill, though he was quieter over it. Ho is taking them yet and going on capitally. Then, there is my cousin, Alice Ann Wilkinson, who lives at Bailiffe Bridge, and my sister Annie, who lives here, they both take theca. My mother suffered from palpitation of the heart, and she is quite free from it now." In this one family, therefare, the same remedy proved a cure for several different ailments. But nothing is more sommon than this. for Dr. Williams pink pills act in quite a different way to ordinary medicine. Ordinary medicine combats the signs and symptoms of disease. Dr. Williams' pink pills attack the foundations ot disease, and eradicate them from the system,not,lacwever,by the wedstwag process of purging or moving the bowels (as so-cstled blood-purifiers do)but by giving direct strength aed nourishment to the blood and nerves. Thus it is that they are able to cure so many different disorder'', among which may be named consumption, bronchitis, paralysis. rheumatism, St. Vitas' dance, nervous prostration, eczema and skin eruptions, and the characteristic ailments of ladies. Sold by all chemists, but if a substitute is offered (the genuine pills always bear the full name Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people) it is tatter to send direct to Dr. Williams' Medicine Company,Holborn Viaduct. div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
ST. HELENS v. OPENSHA.W. LA.NC&SHIRE COUNTY CHAMPIONSEIIP.

St. Helens on Tuesday night met Openshaw, a Man- chester team of some reputation, in the second round of the Lancashire Water Polo Championship. The game was played in the St. Helens bathe, before a large audi- ence. In the 'first round, Openshaw were fortunate enough to secure a bye, while the Saints defeated Man- chester Swan by 7 goals to 2. Both clubs made one alteration in their advertised teams, W Walter playing in place of T. Green for Sr,. Helens, and W Simpson filled the vacancy cawed by the absence of M Brown for Openshaw. At 8.30 the following players entered the Water-7A. Helens : J Aspinwall (Lauce- shire County), goal ; J Bietton (Lancashire County) and W Preston, full backs ; P Ripley (captain) half-back ; W Walker, J Mavity, ani JLe wreizs, forward i Oeen- shaw F Lowe (Lancashire County), gal; W Simp- son and T Mitchell, full backs ; E Bailey, half-back ; G Bradley, AEd vvards, and S Hague, forwards. Referee, Mr W Beattie, Manchester; timekeeper, Mr R Harrison, Openshaw. Ripley lost the toss, and Open Olavr elected to defend the deep end in the first half. In the meaning swim Edwards reached the ball before Mavity, but the visitors failed to use this advantage. The play was very evenly cuntested, the hall travelling quickly from player to player. A passing movement was organised by Ripley, and carried on by Bretton, Preston, and Lawrenson, who, after an exciting tussle in the Opensnaw goal, drew first blood by defeating Lowe in fine style. On resuming, Hague again missed another chance of scoring, as also did Ripley. A-passing movement between Bretton, Mavity, and Walker re- sulted in the latter banding to Lawrenson,who put on No 2. Mavity got the ball first now,and after Ripley tricking his man, gave to Lawrenson, who performed the" hat trick." Nothing further was scored up to the interval, when St. Helene led by 3 goals ti nil. The opening play in the second half was very evenly contested. Lawren- son swain off and passed to Mavity. who handed to Rip- ley, and he banged the leather to Lowe, who cleared. Mavity neat got the ball and swain down the bath in fine style, and finished up by defeating Lowe for the fourth time. After this the Saints continually peppered the Open- shaw goal, but for a long time. they were unsuccessful. Ripley, with spleedid b tclt-t-troded shots, struck the posts several times, as also did Preston, Walker, and Lawrenson. Just before the finish Ripley received, tricked his opponent (Edwards), and scored a grand goal with a low bouncing shot. Final result : St. Helens 5 goals, Openshaw nil. St. Helens now raeet I Ecerton, whom they last week defeated in the Northern Centre Championship by 4 goals to 3, in the aerial-final of the Lancashire County.

ME EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 11, 1899.
A VISIT TO THE "LAND 0' CAKES." [By " QUILP N."'

For the second time I have journeyed beyond the border during a brief respite from work in the smoky atmosphere of Warrington and returned re- freshed by the invigorating breezes of the North. I have seen the canny scot at hams; I have tas:ed his oat cakes but not his whisky ; I have done my level best to twirl R's and give the Scatchman's gutteral " och " with varying success; and I have seen as many sights as can be conveni- ently crowded within the space of ten days, but still, like Oliver Twist, I was inclined to cry for " more."

Edinburgh had long loomed large in my imagina- tion and a strong desire possessed me to see some- thing of the Scotch metropolis. Tne opportunity of loin g so pres-eved itself at last and having availed myself of it I raise my hat to the charms of Nlodera Athens and am prepared to wax as enthu- siastic about its beauties as any ....lcotsman. It is the most interesing city, certainly of Scotland. if not of Great Britain. As one takes an itinerary of the ancient portion of the city the mind is carried back to the dim and distant pas', and a tottering ruin or damaged gable remains to tell of some deed of splendour or bloodshed. The very stones of the pavement, if they could but speak,could tell of some stirring episo les in Scottish history. One is struck with the cosmopolitan character of the visitors to Edinburgh, who seem to come from every pert of Europe and America. As you elbow your way up the Canengate which Scott has im- mortalised, or pay a visit to such places as Holyrood Palace, with its memories of Queen Mary; ez Edin- burgh Castle, so often captured and retaken after many a bloody encounter, you meet with all sorts and coaditioos of men. Thera is the Yankee with his slouch hat and tell-tale voice who "guesses " this is the stair by which Darnley and his associates ascended to the royal apartments to assassinate Riccio, dc-pits the fact] that he has already consul- ted his guide book. Teen there is the more polished visitor from the continent, who as he wan- ders through the Chapel Royal, which is all that re- mains of the great church of the monastery of holyro )d, seems t 3 reverence this relic of a time long before Columbus embarked on his voyage of discovery in the West. Or again, there is the well- proportioned Lancashire lady, who as se inspects the apartments of Holyrood Castle, expresses her opinion that if she had been Qoeen Nlary she would have had a different bedr,)om " to that."

Sir Walter Scott has made Edinburgh a subject of his own and has cast a glamour of romance around it which has fired the imagination of his readers. The city is doubly interesting to those who have read his Waverley novels and the visitor is continually coming across eomething which re- calls him to remembrance. And yet it does appear pas-ing strange that it should have been practi- cally left to Englishmen to raise the money neces- sary for the fine gothic monument which raises its head above the rest, and so fittingly perpetuates Scott's memory. It is not within the scope of this article to deal with the historical associations of itclinburgh or its cenneetion with, such great figures as Queen Mary, John Knox and Walter Scott,but a few brief remarks as to how the city strikes the stranger may not prove uninteresting. The eye of the visitor is at, once attracted by the natural beauties of the city. Edinburgh ceuld not be otherwise than beautiful owing to its unrivalled picturesque situation. Princes-street--now ad- mitted to be by those competent to judge—the finest street in the world CORO its ren3wn to its natural advantages. The reader most picture a delightful promenade one mile in length, lined on one side by business premises, clubs and hotels built in the most expensive and attractive style, while on the other side lie picturesque public gar- dens extending to the valley below with beauti- fully designed monuments standing here and there in memory of the city's most gifted sous. On the opposite side of the valley-which originally was a lake or moat—perched above are to be seen the time-honoured castle looking grim and dour, and buildings comprising the "Old Town." The old and new are connected by bridges spanning this valley which is rich in verdure and beauty. This is only one of the many magnificent sights which dis- tinguish Edinburgh. From Calton Hill, Arthur's Seat or from any of the hills which surround the city the landscape is entrancing and in erecting their public buildings, their colleges, their hospi- tals, their museums, and monuments the situation has been chosen with an eye to effect. Nowhere else have I seen public buildings shown to better advantage. There is a grandeur and dignity about them which arrests the onlooker and they are freer from the-begrimed appearance so common to isuildings in large towns. Tall chimneys belching forth large volumes of smoke are very few in num- ber in Edinburgh. It cannot be said to be a manu- facturing centre and yet it contains over a quarter of a million of inhabitants. The leading industries are those of brewing, distilling, blending and priat- ing, in all of which Endinburgh has gained a great reputation. No one can sejourn long in Scotland without being impressed by the great value placed upon education. This has been the most powerful lever in lifting Scotland to its present position and that the Scotsman does not intend to fall behind in the race is evident by the Oucational faeilities which are so liberally provided. In Edinburgh well- equipped institutions abound and the poorest lad possessed with the desire and ability to learn has a chance of securing a first-class education. But after all Edinburgh is a city of extremes. Side by side with beauty, wealth, and everything that tends to make life happy, there is ugliness, wretchedness and extreme poverty. Turning aside from the historical Canongate one enters the most evil-smelling and dirty courts or" closes" as they are termed, the like of which cannot even be found in Warrington. Here human be- ings are huddled together in the minimum of space and the maudlin besottedness of some of the inhabitants is a sorry spectacle. I saw more drunkenness in Edinburgh on a Saturday evening than I have witnessed in Warrington and that is saying a great deal. The system of housing the people is also very much different from that in Lancashire. Families occupy flats, sometimes rising to a height of six and seven etoreys, and to reach them must be a trying ordeal. They are approached by a common stair and the nearer to heaven your storey is situated the cheaper the rent becomes. No drying grounds are possible and the housewife with her usual ingenuity makes use of short poles inter- laced with cord which protrude from the windows and from which the week's wash is displayed to the public gaze. Washing day seems te be on every day of the week for it rarely happens that some article of clothing is not to be seen gaily floating in the breeze above your head. A Scotsman is usually represented in pictures as rollicking in the glory of kilts, but the tourist who looks for such an individual must not be disappoin- ted if he fails to find each an one. As far as I could see the preservation of the kilt is left to the Scottish soldiers. Despite all criticism it must be admitted that a regiment 'wearing the kilt presents a smart and attractive appearance. At the present time the Gordon Highlanders are stationed at Edin- burgh Castle, and one of the sights is to see the Church parade on Sunday morning. Headed by their pipers and band they march to St. Giles Church in their kilts and wind-blown plumes to the delight of the onlookers. Such a display and the remembrance of the heroic assault of these men on the Dargai heights a while ago. quickens the blood a little and serves to draw in recruits. One cannot help noticing the enthusiasm which Scotsmen have for arms, and I very vividly remember the excitement at Edinburgh in connection with the shooting for the Queen's Prize. It was not, how- ever, won by a Scotsman this time, and I was told I that many had given up all attempts; to pronounce the fortunate Guernsey man's name. One is generally reminded on a holiday how small the world is. Whoever would expect to meet a representative of the" good old town" ,so far north as Edinburgh? And yet as I rambled near the castle, whom should I meet but a well-known Warrington town councillor and his wife My sur- prise was still greater, when on the following day I saw the figure of a leading partner of a Warring- ton firm of ironworkers walk across the shadow of the Scott monument. But Warrington has a still stronger link with Edinburgh in two Warring- ton families who have removed there in connection with the glass trade. Another great advantage possessed by Edinburgh is that it is within easy distance of the coast. A three miles run on the tramway cars—which bye the bye are shortly to run on cables—brings you to Portobello. This is a popular seaside resort, very much like New Brighton without lie Eiffel Tower. There is an abundance of sand which the children revel in and build castles upon which every succeed- ing tide ruthlessly sweeps away. A promenade stretches for considerably over a mile,but the houses and business premises have been built so near the shore that the effect has been completely spoiled.

There is little that is picturesque about the place and a bottle works and pipe manufactory detract from any beauty it possesses. To visit Edinburgh without inspecting the world famed Forth Bridge would be to forego one of the most enjoyable excursions it is possible to have. The bridge is best seen from the water. A pleasant sail -from Leith on the heaving bosom of the Firth of Forth brings you beneath one of the greatest triumphs of modern engineering. As you gaze on the highest bridge in the world, stretching across a broad expanse of one and a fifth of a mile, you admire the symmetry which characterises the whole and appreciate to the full the progress which has been made in bridge-building by Scotch engineers.

'Within a short distance of the bridge is Dalmeny Park, the seat of the Earl of Rosebery. I took ad- vantage of the privilege to walk through the exten- sive and charming grounds, and despite the heat I thoroughly enjoyed the walk of five or six miles which the demesee covers. Dalmeny House occu- pies a prominent position in the centre and is a plain, substantially built residence. It has been visited by Royalty on many occasions and was one of the places the late Mr. Gladstone was delighted to visit. The Park Ranger whom I:met as I wended my way through the well-wooded park and who has seen over 50 years ef service on the estate was full of reminiscences of the distinguished people he had seen there. He spoke with glee of the manner in which Mr. Gladstone felled a giant tree during one of his visits. " The old gentleman," be said," just appeared like a woodman. His jacket and waist- coat were thrown aside and a belt was as curely fastened round his waist. The park resounded with the whack of his axe and was continued at short intervals until the tree fell with a crash to the ground." As compensation for the one he had laid Low Mr. Gladstone planted another which is now railed off and a tablet states the date when it was planted. Trees have also been planted in close proximity by the Prince of Wales, the Duke of York and other notable people. I have a vivid recollection of a pleasant after- noon's visit to Rosh!' and Hawthornden. Both places are delightfully situated within easy reach of Elinburgli aro the historicil castle and abbey at Rosli:n are additional attractions. Very little remain', of the castle but as a guide with a lantern in his hand conducts you through the dungeons and explains everything in connection with the castle you become deeply in- terested in the place. Dating balk to the 12-h cen- tury,the castle has been twice captured and once des- troyed by fire. A peculiar fact in connection with the building of the solid stone walls of the/ castle is the use of oyster shells instead of mortar. It speaks well for the durability of the shells that they have been able to weather centuries of storm and strife and still remain fulfilling their purpose. In order that we may not be unduly elated at our improve- ments introduced into large buildings it may be as well to state that lifts and speaking tubes were in use in this castle generations ago. The "land of Burns " ia not generally visited by tourists in Scotland, but I must ask the reader's indulgence whilst I refer to a brief visit to Mauch- line and Mossgiel in Ayrshire. It was here that the poet Burns spent a por- tion of his life and penned some of his most soul- stirring lines. As one surveys the beautiful scenery and rustic surroundings he begins to realise some- what where Burns received his inspiration. Words- worth gives a glimpse of the scene in the following lines :

" There. said a stripling. pointing with meet pride Towards a low roof, with green trees half-concealed. 'ls Mossgiel farm; and that's the very field Where Burns ploughed up the daisy.' Far and wide A plain below_ stretched seaward, while descried,

Above sea clouds, the peaks of Arran rose ; Ani by that simple notice, the repose Of earth, sky, sea, and air was vivified. Beneath 'the random bield of clod or stone'. 111yriads of daisies have shone forth in flower Near the lark's nest . and in their natural hour Have passed away, less happy than the one That by the unwilling ploughshare died to prove The tender charm of Poetry and Love." Despite the close connection of Burns with Mauchline it was not until quite recently that a memorial was erected in honour of his genius. A fine tower in the Scottish Baronial btyle of archi- tecture ha s now been erected on a site between Mauchline and Mossgiel,and in connection with the memorial hal f-a-dozen cottage homes have b een provided for the use of those in need of a helping hand, and on whom fortune has not smiled. In the basement of the tower there is a museum containing a most interesting collection of relics of Burns. Of all the memorials which Scotland has erected to the memory of its favourite poet this seems to most fittingly perpetuate his memory and put into prac- tice one of the poet's warm-hearted do3trines of sympathy and help in cases of suffering and sor- row. The memorial waich is national in its char- acter was initiated .by. the Glasgow-Manchline Society, and it is largely due to the devoted and untiring efforts of Mr. Thomas Kiln% the hon. treasurer,that the money for providing the memorial and endowing the homes has been raised. A small sum 118 still needed to complete the endowment fund. The Warrington Caledonian Association, I learnt, did not respond to the appeal for assistance, and if the consciences of its members are pricked by recollecting it, there is still time to make amends by empowering the secretary to forward a subscription to this deserving institution. I had a desirA to describe some of the beautiful places in the district of Mauchline, and notably, Ballochmyle' but space forbids, and I mast be coutent to allow my remarks to remain in the inkwell until a more favourable opportunity. I concluded my brief visit at Glasgow, where the burry and bustle and noise inseparable from the great metropolis of the West was in striking con- trast to the peaceful scenes I had left behind in Ayrshire.

div.head: DEATH OF A WARRINGTON GROCER.
div.p: DEATH OF A WARRINGTON GROCER.

The death took place early on Sunday morning of Mr. Thomas Atherton,who for many years carried on the business of general grocer in Glaskell-street. The deceased had been indisposed only a few days, and no idea was entertained that serious symptoms would develop so rapidly and end fatally. Mr. Atherton was well known in the town. He was about 36 years of age, and leaves a widow and five children. The interment took place on Wednesday at the Ceccetery. W. T.
