SO HE WAS INFORMED.—Greene: "Whom are your children said to take after, Mr. Enpeck ?" Enpeck (with a mental reservation): "The younger, with a sweet smile and angelic temper, takes after his mother. The elder, that sullen. looking young viper, takes after me, I'm in- formed."

"WELL, little chap," said the stranger in the family picking up one of the children' what are you going to be when you're a man ?" "Nuflin'," said the child. " Nothing ? Why?" asked the stranger. "Because," said the child, "I'm a little girl." HAVE you ever heard the crocus crow? Or seen where the cowslip slips? Have you ever seen the snowballs snow? Or been where the snowdrop drips? Have you sat in the morning's glory glow t Or attempted to kiss tulips? • A NEW DANGER.—First tramp: "I hear dere s a new drug whut kin be put in a cup of coffee an' it'll take away yer desire fer liquor widout yer Irnowin' it." Second Tramp: "Great hevings ! Some of dem women temperance cranks 'II be tryin' dat game on us !" AMELIA : "Swear not by the moon the incon- stant moon." Augustus: "Then what shall I swear by ? " Amelia: "Swear by that which you hold invaluable; something that you cannot live without." Augustus: "Then, Amelia, I love 'you ! I swear it by my salary." A CHIP OF THE OLD BLOCK.—" Hear Me !" cried the old gipsy, passionately. "Twenty-two years ago I stole the earl's infant from his cradle and substituted my own child !" "Do you mean to tell me," asked the family lawyer, in amaze- ment, "that the young Lord Dontthink is not the son of the earl ? ' "He is not !" replied the gipsy, earnestly. Wrapped in thought, the lawyer paced the floor for several minutes. Then he turned scornfully towards the gipsy. "Away, woman, with your false tale !" he cried. "The young Lord Dontthink is the true heir. If he were not the son of the earl, how could he have inherited the family stupidity ? " The gipsy departed, muttering that she hadn't thought of that.

"YES, I repeat it, marriage makes a man better and kinder. And the proof :—Statistics show that SO per cent. of the convicts are single men." "But, my dear, your reasoning is wrong. Your statistics show only how many men prefer prison to mar- riages." YOUNG POET: "You read my little poem, Mr. Sheerce ?" Editor: "Yes. It was quite pathetic. It excited considerable comment in the office. The boy who attends to s uch matters informs me that it was the first poem he ever burned which was so full of tears as to put the fire out." GOT HOLD OF IT. —A family was discussing music when one member strove to recall the name of a certain composer. "I can't remember it to save my life," she said, "although it is on my tongue's end. As near as I can come to it his name is doorknob." "Doorknob !" repeated one of the others. "There's no composer whose name sounds anything like that. I'll go over a few names: Beethoven, Mendelssohn, Wagner, Haydn, Handel "—" That's it," interrupted the forget- ful one. "ft's Handel. I know it was something you seized with your hands." ON THE OTHER FOOT.—" Congratulate me, mother! Congratulate me, Lizzie!" exultantly exclaimed John Loveluck, bursting in upon his mother and sister. "Ruth Sweetley has accepted me, and I'm the happiest man alive !" "Why, John !" simultaneously exclaimed his hearers. "We hardly know her, you know." "Yes, I know; but she is the dearest, sweetest, loveliest girl in the world," said John Loveluck ; "and I want you to go with me to call on her to-morrow afternoon." " U'm-m ! I don't think I can go to-morrow," said his mother. "And I'm sure I can't," said Lizzie. "Th)ther," said John. "Can't you arrange it somehow?" "I'm sure she's a nice girl," said his mother. "I know my John wouldn't engage himself to anyone his mother wouldn't. approve of." "Of course not," said John. "I don't see why you are in such a hurry to have us call on her," said Lizzie. "You'll marry her whether we like her or not." "Approve of her? Like her?" said John. "Why, I want to know whether she likes you !" LIBERAL, BUT DISCREET.—" I want something handsome in the way of a clock," he said to the jeweller. "We have a very fine line of goods," was the response, "and the prices are very moderate." "I don't care anything about the price. I want something that will show at a glance that it cost a whole lot of money." "Certainly. We have some beautiful imported goods." "That's the idea— something that came from abroad. . I want an onyx pedestal and ormolu trimmings and a statue on top of it." "Here's a veritable work of art." "That's pretty well; but I'd like something more attractive than that. It's to be a birth- day present to my wife. We haven't been keeping house very long, and she's been wor- ried for fear people would think we were going without a clock because we couldn't afford one. I'm going to see that she has some- thing so handsome that it'll dazzle everybody who comes into the parlour, and so precious that it has to be kept under glass like a specimen in the museum." "How is this one?" the jeweller in- quired, as he lifted a massively ornate article from a shelf. "That's the very thing. That'll please her almost to death. Pack it up and send it to my house and send the bill to my office." "It'll cost twenty pounds," the jeweller mildly suggested." "That's all right. It looks as if it were worth it." He started for the door, but came back and said: "By the way, you'd better give me another clock—one of these small, nickel-plated affairs that cost about five shillings, so that we can stick it in an obscure ccrner to look at when we want to know what time it is." -

BILLINGS Y. HOADLY.—Billings and Hoadly on tha train home the other evening became involved in an argument over the respective abilities of their wives as marketers. "Mr. badly," Billings said, "let me assure you, sir, that I fully concur with you regarding the ability of Mrs. Hoadly to market; but, sir, Mrs. Billings displays such remarkable sagacity in her purchases that I have never yet had an occasion to question the advisability of one." Hoadly's cheeks puffed out for a moment before he replied: "Well, Billings, I would not for the world question such excellent judgment as that of Mrs. Billings, especially when I think of her tasty little dinners, but did I ever tell you of Mrs. Hoadly's experience with a market butcher? I have always thought it the smartest example of marketing I ever encountered. You remember Pork6ides, the butcher, who keeps a stall near the lower end of the market?" "I have heard Mrs. Billings comment upon that person." Yes, it was Mrs. Billings that recommended, him to Mrs. Hoadly, and this day, wishing to buy some spring chickens, it occurred to her to try Porksides, so she inquired: "'How many spring chickens have you got to-day, Mr. Porksides?' " I have just six left,' said he; there they are hanging on the hooks.' "Now here is where Mrs. Hoadly excelled in astuteness ;" and Hoadly's face beamed proudly as he told it. " I'll take three of them, she said ; 'betas I keep a boarding- house, I want you to pick out the three toughest. Possibly you can let me have them for a little less.'" "Bah !" exclaimed Billings. "You don't call that astutensss, do you ?' " Wait a minute, my dear Billings. Porksides went to work punching those chicks till he had selected the three toughest. Just as he finished in walked your wife, Mrs. Billings. " Altar the two ladies had greeted each other, my wife turned, and to the utter astonishment of Porksides, totally disregarding the three tough chickens he had selected for her, coolly informed him that she would take the other three. Now what do you think of that method of securing tender chickens?" "A smart one, Hoadly ; yes indeed, quite clever—in fact, almost as clever a thing as Mrs. Billings would do. But then it would be difficult for any butcher to fool her on chickens." Hoadly had been laughing so hard over his story that it was a moment or two before he realised what Billings had said. When he did he sadly shook his head and relapsed into thought for a moment. "Billings," he finally said, "there was only one person in that trans- action I felt sorry for." " Who? Porksides?" "No, old man, it was you." "Me ! What on earth did I have to do with it?" "Well, you see, Billings, your wife bought the three tough chickens."

WARRISGION BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.
A JOCOSE DEFENDANT.

At the Nisi Prius Court, St. George's Hall, on Saturday afternoon, Mr. Justice Bigham and a com- mon jury heard an action for damages for breach of promise and seduction, brought by Jessie Mather, of Padgate, against Maurice If. Royston. Mr. Rigby Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Horridge represented the defendant. Mr. Swif t said defehdaut was a partner in tbe firm of William Roystou and Co., chemical manufac- turers. Both parties resided at Padgate, near War- rington, and in August, 1893, the plaintiff, who was then about fifteen years or age, went as domestic servant to the house of Mrs. Royston, the defend- ant's mother She remained there from 1893 up to January, 1893. During the first two or three months nothing took place, but subsequently defendant began to take notice of her. One day Plaintiff was winding some wool on pegs, when Mrs. Royston and defendant passed through the room, and the former suggested that the latter should "help Jessie to wind it." He did so, and when the work was done he kiseed her, wed exclaimed, " What a dear little girl you are !" Atten this defendant used to meet her as she came from church, and took her for walks. About Mar, 1897 he offered to marry her, but was anxious that it should be kept secret from the I knowledge of his family. In January, 1898, plaintiff left Mrs. Royston'e, and went home for a little while. On her leaving he accompanied her on his bicycle, carry- ing a hat-box, and on the following Sunday he met her with her father. He then handed her a letter which he said he intended to post for her. In March, 1898, plain- tiff went into the service of Mrs. Stephenson' of War- rington, and whilst there defendant took her out for walks. In Easter, 1898, intercourse took place between them. She remonstrated with him at the time, but he replied that it was all right as he was going to marry her. The intercourse continued until it was found that plaintiff was pregnant, when she left Mrs. Stephenson's. She then wrote to him, acquainting him of her con- dition, as a result of which ne had an interview, in the I course of which he said. " Y, u must give me time to ' see what is to be done." The next day, 30th Septem- ber, he wrote a letter, in which he stated that, whether rightly or wrongly, be must take the responsibility upon hin.self to shield Jessie. It would be best for her to it ave home, and keep the fact to themselves. He added that the mischief could be lived down; that to suffer a life of misery by doing some- thing which might be most honourable he could not, as he had still " somethiug in the way." The next night he went to her house,and suggested that she should go to Crewe till the matter was over. Her parents, however, refused to assent to this course. Then for the first time he said he did net intend to marry her, and said that if he bad suggested marriage "it was all in fun." Sabse- quently, in December, she wrote to him to see her at her house. He went, and defendant had an interview with plaintiff's father, and asked," How much will you take to settle it ?" The father replied. " A hundred pounds won't settle it." Defendant said," A hundred pounds is a lot of money, but I have a lady friend who will give me £5O, and I can raise another £50." The father told her that that would net do, but Mrs. Roe's- , ton's counsels prevailed, and in order to avoid a scandal I plaintiff's people agreed to receive £lOO. The next day he raid he had seen the lady whom he thought would give him £5O, and she had said that " if they were not satisfied with £5O they had better try what they could I get." In February the child was born. A summons was I taken cut before tbemagistrate3, and an order was made lupon him to par 43 per week. Before the magistrates the defendant admitted the seduction. Plaintiff, an intelligent young woman, corroborated her counsel's opening statement as to the defendant promising her marriage and taking advantage of her. Whilst defendant was in Manchester be wrote to her several times, but she had not preserved the letters. She went on her holidays in July, 1898, and not anticipating that she would be deceived, she burnt the letters before leaving. In these letters he addressed her as " his dear pet," " his darling," and used ether endearing expres- sions. Cross-examined by Mr. Horridge the time she burnt the letters plaintiff was aware of her condition. She denied that the intercourse took place in the defend- ant's mother's house. From first to last he had offered to pay for the child. Joseph Mather, engineer, Padget', father of the also gave corroborative evidence. He saw the defendant and told him about the condition of his danghter, and said that the most honourable thing he could do was to carry out his promise, and marry his daughter. Defendant replied that he could not if the angels came down from heaven, as he had already two " observations "ti view. Mr. Swift said he rather thought the defendant meant "obstructions," and that he had two of them in view. His Lordship : si very awkward position. (Laughter.) Witness added that the defendant never denied that he promised when the metter was mentioned. Matilda Ellison, of Manchester, a friend of both parties, said she had seen letters addressed to plaintiff from defendant, in one of which he commenced : "My dearest Jessie," aed concluded, " Yours ever, Maurice." This was the plaintiff's case. Maurice H. Royston, the defendant, examined by Mr. Horridge, said he was . not a partner. His father died in 1897, and his mother had the business passed on to her. Be was employed in the business at a salary of £25 a year. Be receive-, board and lodgings, and lived at home. There was no premise of marriage, and there never had been any promise. At the interview with the father no suggestion was made about his ever having promised to marry, but Mrs. Mather afterwards stated as an honourable man he ought to marry her daughter. He said he would go home and consider the matter, which he did, and wrote the letter which bad been read. He afterwards saw the plaintiff, and told her that her father had said he pro- mised to marry her. She said he did not promise. The father eming upon the scene said, " But I will see to that." In cross-examination by Mr. Swift, he admitted that he had already sworn before the Revising Barrister that be was a partner in the firm, but said it was for a vote, and he did not think it was a serious matter. Mr. Swift: You have also put up as a Parish Coun- cillor, Mr. Royston ? Defendant: A bit of a joke. Someone put metup. Mr Swift: Oh, that was a joke, too. Your are rather iond of joking. (Laughter.) In further cross-examination, defendant said that his firm hod also brought an action in the Warrington County Court against another firm, and lost it. He admitted that the judge then said that his evidence was not worthy of belief. Ile was not well at the time. Mr. Swift : Are you well to-day (Laughter) ? Defendant ; Yes, quite well, thank you. (rtenewed laughter.) In reply to the learned judge, defendant said he never wrote anything that could be misconstrued and con- sidered affectenate. In answer to Mr. Swift, defendant denied having ever asked if £lOO would settle the case. Mr. Horridge, for the defence, said if the jury thought the defendant was responsible, it might se a case for damages. There had been no proof of his means. The jury bad seen the sort of half-baked creature the defend- ant looked in the hex. (Laughter.) Mr. Swift, on behalf of the plaintiff, said he hoped the jury would make the defendant suffer for what he had looked upon as a jlke. His Lordship, in addressing the jury, advised them to give reasonable damages, because if they gave excessive damages they might not be recovered. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff, and awarded damages £l5O.

div.head: AUGUST 11th 1899.
div.p: AUGUST 11th 1899.

WITH the ending of the The Session. session Comes the beginning of political forecasts. Everybody asks whether the Urovernment is as strong as it was in Feb- ruary, and whether the Opposition is any stronger. Estimates of men and measures abound. The truth seems to be that the session has had two or three significant effects. The day before it assem- bled, February 6th, the Liberal members met at the Reform,Club to consider what should be done as Sir WILLIA3I HARCOURT had resigned his posi- tion as Leader of the Opposition, and Sir H. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN was unanimously selected in his place, so that, after the reading of the QUEEN'S Speech, he had to justify his selection, and this he did in a speech full of fight and plea- sant chaff. A second effect may be seen in the fewer attacks on the Government policy in China, as the outcome of the Anglo-Russian agreement, signed April 29th. The agreement with France about the Bahr-el-Ghazal has also served to lessen debate. The gradual devel- opment of a critical situation in the the Transvaal has shown some division amongst the Liberals, but it has increased the cohesion of Ministerialists. The most remarkable effect of the session, however, has been the growth of dis- approval of the domestic policy of the Government • Sir H. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN'S attack at the Corn xnencemeat stirred up the Government to appoint a committee on old-age pensions, the Tithes Bi compelled Mr. G. WHITELEY to pass over to the Liberal side of the House, and the augmented expenditure and the rather tricky measures to meet it have caused much discontent. The Ritualist question has also divided the Ministerial ranks. No one will venture to say that the ses- aion has strengthened the Government, and its close finds the Liberals in excellent spirits and getting ready for the General Election. Until the session opened it had been rather doubtful whether the Government would venture to deal with London government. The Queen'sl Speech soon settled the matter by giving it prom- inence. No other first-class measure was promised, but the catalogue of minor bills included a Small Dwellings Bill, a Food and Drugs Bill, a Factory Act Amendment Bill, a Money-Lending Bill, a Companies Bill, and a Board of Agriculture for Ireland and a Board of Education for England There were some amendments to the Address, of the customary type. One about the taxation of land values was only defeated by 24 votes, and Mr. REDMOND'S attempt to entangle parties by a statement about Home Rule was defeated by SOO to 43. There was a great show of Government activity at starting. The Money-Lending Bill was introduced early by Lori JAMES, but it never reached the Commons. The Lord CHANCELLOR'S Companies Bill had the same fate. Mr. RITCHIE'S Automatic Coupling's Bill did not long survive, and a commission to enquire took its place. The London Government Bill was introduced February 23rd, and by July 13th it had passed the House of Lords. Its career in the Commons Was rather chequered. Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE Made the longest speech he has ever delivered in the Commons, in moving the rejection of the bill O n its second reading, and his amendment was de- feated by 245 to US votes, March 24th. There Was a considerable struggle in Committee, and the result of it was that the whole of the boroughs to be created were scheduled and the interests of the Lendon County Council were better safeguarded. The question of women as councillors and alder- men underwent many changes, and was left to the Report, whenthey were allowed to be both. But the Lords struck out the permission, and when the bill returned to the Commons the House acquies- ced by a considerable majority. There hardly seemed to be any chance of much further fierce controversy, when, the Government availing itself of the Ten Minutes Rule, intended for non-contentious measures, Mr. Lorre, intro- duced the Tithes Bill, paying half the local rates out of local taxation of all tithe-rent-charge attached to a benefice,making the clergy a- pi-737isrit of £87,000 a year. The bill was hurried forward. The first reading was carried by 247 to 169 votes, and the second reading by 315 to 177. It was (plickly got into Committee, and by means of the Closure rule it was run through this stage in four Sittings without any amendment whatever. Not only did Mr. 'WHITELEY attack it from the Govern- teent side and afterwards join the Liberals, but, the Oldham election, the Unionist as well as the Liberal candidates declared against it, and as the two seats were contested—ono vacant by death and the other by resignation—it was no surprise to any observer of the signs of the times when the Liberals, Mr. EMMOTT and Mr. RINCIMAN, Were returned. This was the biggest blow the Government has ever had. The St. Pancras election, by a reduced Unionist olajority,also testified to the damage the Govern- °lent had received by this clerical relief or dole bill. The clergy are to receive half their rates from the Local Texation Fund until 1901, when the measure expires. The finance of the Govern- meat has been altogether bad, and the Tithes Bill Was only one sample. The Chancellor of the Ex- chequer found himself with an expenditure of £112,927,000 to face and an income of only £1.10,287,000. He suspended a portion of the N'ational Debt Service to get two millions, on the ground that in some years to come annuities would fall in which some other Government might mis- use,and he obtained by an alteration in the Stamp Duties, and the duties on foreign and colonial Wines, the difference he required, leaving him a

surplus of a quarter of a million. But this has long since vanished owing to other expenditure, and how the national account stands now no one , seems to know. Naval and military expenditure are higher, there was a grant to Lord KITCHENER of £30,000, money has been found for the Imperial Institute, for loans to the colonies, and for several other raqtters. The general financial muddle is remarkable. Ritualism has been much to the front. There have been several debates npon it, though the Government seemed to be most anxious to avoid anything of the kind. There was an Amendment to the Address in the Commons on the subject, whicri was defeated by 221 to 89 votes. The memorial of the English Church Union provided another opening for discussion, and its statements were Eo extraordinary that the House was bound to censure them, which it did by 200 votes to 14, the CECIL family being in the minority. On the Church Discipline Bill, introduced by 111 r. MCARTHUR, there was an animated debate, and the ATTORNEY-GENERAL moved and carried by 310 to 155 an amendment which is likely to be heard of again. Whilst declining to sanction a measure which created new offences, the House of Commons declared that if the off 'its now being made by the Archbishops and bishops to secure the duo obedience of die clergy are not speedily effectual further legislation will be required to maintain the due observance of the existing laws of Church and Realm." Now that the Lambeth judgment on incense and lights, con demning both, has been given, and other decisions are soon expected, it will be possible to see what legislation, if any will be needed.

The miscellaneous bills of the session include the Telephone Bill, which has had a chequered career, Mr.ROBSON'S Half-Timers' Bill, and bills to buy out the Niger Company, to provide seats for female shop assistants, and to enable local bodies to ad- vance money to workmen and others anxious to buy small houses. The list of massacred infants is ,unusually hrge. Yet the Government has crushed private members to the wall, taken their time, and only two oi their measures survive. Debates have taken place on the Indian Sugar Bill, the Mandi's head, the Transvaal, Wei-hai-wei, and several other subjects. The death of Mr. T. E. ELus, the senior Liberal Whip, during Easter, was a sad event, and when Mr. HERBERT GLAP- STONE consented to act in his place there was general relief. More spirit has been infused into the Opposition, and Sir H. CAMPBELL-BANNER- MAN'S leadership, though much abused in some quarters, has been an undoubted success. Mr. BRonnicK has proved a capable Under- Secretary for Foreign Affairs. In other respects there has not been much that is personal to record. The deaths of Lard HERCHELL and the DUKE of BEAUFORT served to show of what diverse material:, he House of Lards is composed. There is a general impression that one more session will see the close of the present Parliament.
As we shall hear a Parataeuntcy in South good deal about the Africa.

paramountcy of Great Britain in South Africa during the next five months,it may be convenient to ascertain what is meant by the term in the mouths of some active, if not militant, politicians. There is a false and a real meaning to the word. Sometimes it is meant to imply that the Transvaal and the Free State are, or ought to be, suppressed, as wielding a power that is adverse to that of Eng- land, and as plotting to maintain the over-lordship of the Dutch against the English and the natives. It is used in an offensive, minatory fashion, in- tended to be irritating, and perhaps insulting. We have no sympathy with any such employment of an expressive phrase. But there is another and a real sense in which paramountcy expresses what cannot be conveyed in any other way. The Cape was originally a Dutch settlement, but there can be no question that from the Zambesi to the sea British power has been dominant for some time, and must be preserved in very much the same form in which it now is. We have had to extend our influence, and to destroy all threatening combinations of natives and of native States. There is no longer any armed and disciplined Kaffir Power within reach, and the military power of this country has been exhibited in destroying them. The Zulus the Basutos, and the Matabele, as independent fighting forces, have ceased to exist. It would be incorrect to say that these people have been exter- minated, or that they would not once more be come a considerable military power in the hands either of the English or the Dutch, to be used by the former against the latter, or by the latter against the former, as desperate circumstances might necessitate. At any rate, the various Kaffir tribes, recognisable by definite names, or merely known as Kaffirs,are numerous enough and scattered enough to constitute a considerable danger to British citizens and settlers if they once believed they could kill and raid them with the protecting support of an enemy. What is it keeps thes people quiet, prevents their organisation into fighting bodies, and teaches them to respect the Englishman ? The belief in our military strength, in our superiority as a civilised Power—in a word, in our paramountcy. It occurs to us that this side of a real danger is frequently lost sight of when sentimental considerations are urged against a policy which is believed to be needlessly offensive. Vet it is obvious that if the Kaffirs once get the notion that the Afrikanders ot Cape Colony and the neighbouring States on the Orange River and across the Vaal are able to dictate to this country, to control its diplomacy, and to carry the day, there will be no safety for any English settlennnts remote from military garrison centres. If we will sometimes think of this aspect of the matter we shall not push criticism so far as to create the belief that we are eager to be submissive to the Dutch, and that whoever does not approve of everything they do and say is not a patriot but a Jingo. If we will do this a considerable danger will be avoided, and we may keep our heads cool.

Scene very important subjects will be discussed at the autumnal gathering of the Associated Chambers ef Commerce at Belfast next month. Several Chambers are desirous that stronger pres- sure than ever should be put upon the Govern- ment to introduce the compulsory use of the me- tric system of weights and measures. This would be of benefit in foreign trade, but at home it would entail immense confusion, and not a little expense. In any case, we imagine it is far too early for any Government to attempt to fix a defi- nite date, as suggested by Birmingham, after which the usa of these measures shall be obliga- tory. To begin with a more thorough education in the metric system is necessary at school, and pre- haps, also, the Government departments might be- gin to familiarise the country with the system by adopting it. The system will come by-and-bye, and, though it will be distinctly useful, it would be unwise to force the pace unnaturally. The sug- gestion that the Government should make equally

div.head: EXAMINEE, FRIDAY AUGUST 11, 1899
div.p: THE EXAMINEE, FRIDAY AUGUST 11, 1899

liberal grants for commercial subjects as are at pr2sent given to the science objects in all schools is only reasonable. The great need of the times is for systematic commercial education, not the hap- hazard book and paper instruction which very often passes current in small local schools. Simi- larly, the State might well encourage the teaching of modern languages in secondary schools. Unfor- tunately, at present, the State encourages many things that are better left undeveloped alto- gether.

There is a differe:ace of opinion about gipsies. The townspeople who occasionally spend holidays in the country, and have sentimentalised over Borrow's book, find an ecstatic delight in a camp fire and a dirty caravan on a village green. The neighbouring farmer who misses some chickens, and is unable to put his finger on the offender, takes a severer view of these Romany descendants. The mind of the one class is filled with a sense of the picturesque; the mind of the other with a confused impression about the poultry. Both beliefs are exaggerated distortions of fact, for it not infrequently happens that the travellers are both vulgar and honest. There are, however,still left in the rural districts some few wanderers who give us ideas of what old English life was like. We have no antiquary employing his days, as in Sir Walter Scott's historical novel, in restoring the graves of the Covenanters. Most of the ancient tombs in our counti, y churchyards are moss-covered, or bear now only the blurring hand- print of Father Time. But there are still quaint figures that redeem dull scenes and revive tradi- tions of those days before machinery made agricul- tural work nearly as uninteresting as a modern cotton loom. The thatchers who pass from farm to farm are wonderful old men, some of them, and just now in the hop-gardens of the South of Eng- land are a delightful couple who prepare the cbar- coal which is put on the plants. They make the wood into a mound, as mysterious to the unaccus- tomed eye as the Roman earthworks, and then they start trio fire in the centre, which slowly transforms the mass into charcoal. For three days and nights they take turns in watching the process, with a carp worthy of an alchemist, and they sleep as may be in the open air, with the stars for night-lights. The man is four score years and hale and hearty ; the woman is threescore and ten. They know nothing about sanitary dwellings, or new hygienic rules for longevity; but they are never ill, and so don't need them.

We do not suppose that it will cause any "international complication," bub the shooting of a French sailor by the men of the British gun-boat Leda, is an unfortunate affair. Happily the feel- ing between this country and France has not suffered from tension for some time, and the inci- dent off Dungenness on Wednesday will probably affect public opinion very slightly across the Channel. This is all the more likely as the French smack on which deceased was killed was poaching in British waters wken detected by the Leda. A chase ensued. " Froggy " used every device possible to avoid capture, and finally ball cartridge, aimed at the rigging, had to be used to bring him to. An unlucky bullet struck the helmsman dead, and this is what gives the affair its serious aspect. The English captain was quite within his rights, and the fatal termination of the trespass beyond the three mile limit may perhaps have the effect of making the fishermen more observant of the law. Somehow or other trawlers of all nationalities have a very loose code of morality where the three mile limit is con- cerned. They will cross it wherever there appears a safe opportunity, an a possible chase by the watchful gunboat only adds a little sport to the undertaking. But the sport has ended in tragedy, and the fishermen had better take warning.

The number of suicides which actually do take place is large, but it is nothing in comparison with the number of people who are anxious to shuffle off this mortal coil, and would do so were they not too cowardly. Suicide is a speedy way of quitting a world in which life may seem not worth living, but the committal of it has the serious drawback of entailing physical suffering, the contemplation of which is sufficient to deter thousands of persons from the rash act. But few people can have any idea of the num- ber of miserable folk there are who would willingly die were the means to that end suffi- ciently comfortable. A recent incident throws some light on the subject in a startling manner. There was a case heard in a London Police Court in which a physician gave evidence, and referred in the course of his testi- mony to his knowledge of a poison instantane- ous in its action and positively painless. Like a wise man, however, he refused to put the public in possession of his information by telling the Court anything more about it. Since then, and within two weeks, ho has received more than three thousand letters from men and women in London begging the name of the poison! It is difficult to estimate that physician's thankfulness for the wise precaution which apparantly prevented so many suicides.
NELSON-STREET SUNDAY SCIZOOLS.

Through the kindness of t 139 friends atCantden Chapel the ab3ve Sunday School will hold its anniversary at Camden Chapel on Sunday next. The preacher will be the Rev. T. Wilkes, ef eouthpert (and formerly of Run- corn). In the afternoon Mr. B. Brawn, IP.. of Widnes will conduct a meeting. Special music will be rendered by the choir and scholars, and collections will be made in aid of the school fends. ILLTREATING A HORSE AT WIDNES.

Before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday morning, John Cartwright, of Sutton Oak, was charged with working a horse whilst in an unfit condition, and John Wright the owner, was charged with causing the animal to be worked. Police Constable Hegan said he examined the horse in Birchfield-itreet, Sutton. It was attached to a wagornette, and drawing three persons. He found two large wounds the size of a five shilling piece under the collar. Wright was fined 30s and costs, and Cart- wright 10; and costs.

div.head: em0ne..0011080.m...1=111 BRITISH WORKMAN'S AND GENERAL ASSURANCE COMPANY.
div.p: em0ne..0011080.m...1=111 BRITISH WORKMAN'S AND GENERAL ASSURANCE COMPANY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The 33rd annual meeting et this Company was held at the Masonic Hall, New-etreet,Birmingham,laet week, the Chairman of the Directors (Mr. F. T. Jefferson) pre- siding over a large attendance. The Chairman said he rose with great pleasure to propose the adoption of the 33rd annual report. The pleasure of meetieg thma once again was enhanced by the fact that the directors were able to lay before them the most satisfactury report that this or any previ- ous board had been able to present. (Applause.) The fact that they had been able to anew a balance of £85,500 after writing off nearly £6,000, and after charg- ing all valuation department expenses to revenue was the best testimony they could produce to the wisdom of the policy inaugurated by the reformed board, and to the loyalty and zeal with which that policy had been eupported by their large holy of representatives and by the in lnor st:ff. They had added to the Assurance Fund £Bs,soo—(applausel—netwithstanding the fact that they had paid over £33,000 more in claims, and over £3,000 more in eurrenders than in the previous year—(applause). When the reformed board took the reins of office at the close of the financial year 1897, the Assurance Fund stood at £239,536. Toelay—two years after—it stood at £4o6,6s7—(applause)—a marvellous increase of 70 yer cent, in the two years. In fact, during the last two years they had added to the Assur- ance Fund practically the same amount as was added in the nine years previously. In the nine years com- mencing 1888 and endiee 1897 there was added to the funds only £9OO nano than they had added during the last two years. (Applause.) From this they would see that they were rapidly altering the proportion of total fends to the total premium income. In 1697, when they took the reins ef office,the proportien of funds to income was 51 per cent. As a result of twelve months' working ie. 1898 they had increased the proportion tc 64 per cent. To-day they presented the report for 1899, which showed that the proportion had increased to 721- per cent.— (hear, hear.) And they were happy to say that this rapid rise in the proportion of funds to income was not based on a Comparison of funds with a falling, or even stationary, income. They were able to report to-lay the largest increase ever made in the income of the Com- pany within one year. The income had increased this year by £53,687, and that, added to the increase re- ported last year. showed an increase in the two years of nearly £102,060 per annum. (Applause.) Then this did not exhaust the record of progress made. They had not only to report an increase in the funds—the greatest ever made—they had not only to report the largest in- crease ever yet shown in the income, but they had the satisfaction of reporting what he ventured to believe the shareholders would regard as a magnificent net increase in business in force of 74,752 policy holders, producing a new annual premium income of £65,263. (Rear,hear.) And they had again. to congratulate themselves upon the class of business being introduced, showing, as he had the pleasure of stating last year, that the Company was getting hold of a higher class of assurant, proving, as he believed it did prove, that it was the thrifty,industrioue and sober part of the community which was realising the advantages of life .assurance. (Applauee.) The report was unanimously adopted. ----NW-- • PERSONAL.

We understand that Miss Lena Dobson has been engaged to sing on Sundays throughout the season at the Alhambra, Blackpool. The medical faculty report of the University College, Liverpool, has just been published. Among the prizemen is Mr. G. W. N. Joseph, son of Dr. Joseph, of Warrington, who in the summer session gained a medal in materia medicl,and in the winter session a medal in anatomy (descriptive) and a certificate in physiology.

div.head: OPEN-AIR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: OPEN-AIR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.

Widnes Subscription Prize Band, under the conductor- ship of Mr. J. Harper, was the attraction at the Mersey Mission Recreation ground, on Wednesday night, and quite a large number of people availed themselves of the epportunity of hearing the band play " Lohen- grin "(the test piece for the New Brighton Tower Brass Band Contest). Those concerts fill a long felt want, and give a capital opportunity to the young folks of the district which they may utilize for healthful enjoyment.

div.head: PLINKY RIIN'CORN BOY.
div.p: A PLINKY RIIN'CORN BOY.

The Jolley's are well-known in Runcorn as a plucky lot of fellows—and en the foetball field few there 103 who are so much respected. The latest addition to the ex- ploits of the family is the plucky feat of Richard Jolley who resides with his parents in Canal-street. Dick was fishing near Earps Chemical Works and was attending to his rod:and line when he heard a splash. Turning round he saw a little girl named Annie Astle, aged 6 years, in the canal, and though there were numbers of other persons present withaut hesitation Jolley plunged in and rescued the little girl. The gallant little rescuer is but 12 years of age, and has only jut recovered from an attack of typhoid fever. The attention of the Humane Society should be called to this brave little fellow.
UNLAWFITL WOUNDING AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday morning, before the Mayor (Alderman Wareing)and Major L.wis, Peter Andrews, a Pole, was charged with unlawfully wounding and doing grievous bodily harm te John Tobin by striking him on the head with a stone in Water-street on Saturday. July 29. Mr. Simons (inter- preter). of 29, Livingstone-road, Tranmere, examined him. Dr. Edmund Dukes, physician, practising in Widnes, said he saw the injured an at his own LIOUS". He was suffering from a large wound in the 'nip, ex- tending to the boae—a star-shaped wound, ems and a half inches across. He was improving satisfactorily.— Several other witnesses were called, including Police Constable Spence, who said that the prisoner underste,l and could speak English fairly well.—The magistrates committed him to the nest Liverpool QaarLer S3ssious.
ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN TOURIST.

_ An accident occurred on Friday last which might have been attended with much more serious results. Whilst Mr. William Unsworth, son of Mr. J. Unsworth, of Stanley Villas, Runcorn, was on a cycle tour in Scotland with a number of friends, something got wrong with his machine. e got off to attend to i wh:lst his friends went slowly ahead. Having repaired ,he darn ige Mr. Unswerth went in chase of hi triends and it his anxiety to catch up to them failed to notice til3 legend " Dangerous to cyclists "at the top of a steep hill. The resllt was he went do gra the steep at a fearful rate and banged into a wall at the bottom. Mr. tJawar,h wag severely injured and had a very narrow escape. We understand he is much better now and has returned to Runcorn.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATIt AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATIt AT WIDNES.

The sudden death has been reported to the Widnes police, of Mr. Robert Price, 88, Birchtield-road, at the age of 65, years, for a lone ,ime foreman at Mes.as. Gasket' Deacon's Works, Widnee, wnich took place on Sunday evening. About 10 a.m. on Sunday evening deceased left home on his machine, in his usual health, for a ride to gale, returning at 1 p.m. He thou par- took of a hearty dinner, and went to bed. accordirk; to his usual custom on Sunday afternoon. At 5 p.m. he awakened, and took a drink of lemea squaAn. Two minutes later he beckoned to his wife and tuen tell back. When she got to him he was dead. Some years ago deceased had an apoplectic seizure,and tnere is no doubt this has in a great measure been the cause of his death. Deceased was well known ia Widnes, and greatly res- pected.

This place of entertainment is now occupied by Messrs. adigh and Hessey's Novelty Choir and up-to- date Dioramas, and a very good" show "it is too ! Of its kind, few, that have visited Runcorn duenz recent years can eonspare with it. The singing is fair, the in- strumentali4s are good—especially the flute, and those who wish to hear a really good player Ehnuld hear Mr. Hessey ; but, of the pictures thrown ell tha eanvae,they are woaderfully good, and Mr, Hai•zh is to be highly congratulated upon the fine display he produces. The show commences at 8 and is over by 10.15 ; the prices are 2e., Is., 61., and 31., so that a visit is within the means of all.—On Sunday there will be sacred song ser- vicos. Mists Hilda Nielson sang" Good night beloved" on Wednesday, to a fair house, and was well received. Miss Nellie Doreen also received an ovation for " Eileen Alannah " and the coon song 't Honey Darling." Both artistes possess excellent voices, and use them to advan- tage. div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.

[By CORRESPONDENT.] Who is not acquainted with the story of the "Ewe Lamb," and who upon reading it does not feel charitable enough today "it's a shame !" Well I could recount such another story to the members of the Runcorn Fishing Club, and like Natham could say at the finish" Thou art the Men." What the Runcorn Fishing Club are desir- ous of doing is to monopolise all the available fishing ground, and I understand have approached Sir Richard Brooke with a view to getting prohibitive rights to fish in the Bridgevrater Canal. Now I hope Sir Richard will not grant it ; for, many years this bit of free fishing ground—thanks to the generosity of Sir Richard— has been the poor man's "little bit of sugar." Should the club secure their monopoly, there are many who now enjoy a little angling who will be debarred from it by their inability to join the club through financial reasons. Something, however, tells me that Sir Richard will do the fair thing, and if the Fishing Club are allowed to fish as a recog- nised body in the reaches of the canal, nothing will be done to interfere with existing fishers.

The magnificent weather we are now enjoying gives promise of successful harvesting. On all sides of the country operations are being carried out and the whirr of the reapiag machine is the music that greets the ear of those who journey over the country-side. The crops generally present a good appearance,—both in respect to length of straw and grain bearing—and the farmer,granted the weather holds out a trifle longer, should this year be a con- tented man.

On May lah I wrote stating that the old Gas Works at the Sprinch.had been selected as a site for a new industry for quick-silver extraction, and that possibly the work would be commenced within a few days. Something, however, cropped up to militate against the success of the negotiations, and it was thonght they would fall through; still my authority felt so sure of his ground that I gave his statement without reserve. It is satisfactory now, notwithstanding adverse criticism, to refer to the incident, for at length the negotiations havo been successfully carried out.

The "Sons of Temperance" will on Saturday--(to- morrow)—celebrate their jubilee. Forming in pro- cession and headed by the Volunteer Band they will parade Ow principal thoroughfares of the town winding up with an open-air meeting near the Railway Station. A feature of the procession will be the inclusion of the" life boat," which has been obtained with great difficulty.

The August Bank Holiday has passed and only the recollection remains. Runcorn evidently was on its best behaviour, as the sessions for Tuesday last were productive of but two " drunks." Two " drunks " between the whole police force,is indeed a novelty for Runcorn ; but it is evident from the signs of the times that Monday next will make up for it, though the coming celebration of the Sons of Temperance should somewhat tend to diminish the number,

div.head: FIRST BABY FOR 200 YE&R.S.
div.p: FIRST BABY FOR 200 YE&R.S.

For over 200 years no baby has been born on the island of Balta, ono of the far-disi:aat Shetland group. But this long period has now been broken, for the other day, during the recent herring fishing season a young lady hailing from the Buckle (Banffshire) district gave birth to a fine healthy boy in One ot the wooden hots belonging to a curing station. The baby has been christened Salta Geddes Poison, and the laird of the island has presented the mother with a cheque for £25. The fortunate little stranger has also been made the re- cipient of several hundred silver coins of the realm from visitors, who came from all parts to see the young record-breaker.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
LOCAL CASE AT TEE AS3IZES.

At the Liverp)ol Acsiz,s, on Saturday, before Mr. Jus- tice Wilts, Arthur Ireland (20), labourer, was indicted for having on June 25th. at Halewood, assaulted and illtreated a girl named Edith Helen Richardson,daughter of the postmaster at Hate. Prisoner, who was unde- fended, was found guilty and sent to gaol for fifteen months' hard lab3ur. Tug RUNCORN SESSIONS.

Owing to the August holiday no summonses were made returnable for Runcorn Petty Sessions on Tuesday last, with the result that the magistrates had but a light calendar. Mr. F. J. Norman preside3.—James Molyneaux was discovered by Constable Breeze, helplessly drunk in High-street on the sth of August. He was lying en the footpath opposite St. Paul's Chapel. Br3eze considered he would be safest at the Police Station and took him there.—Molyneaux who said he was a labourer at the Runcorn Docks, admitted having two pints, but stated he had been at work—" on duty"—for 19 hours. Fined 5s and costs.—Jaiates Rolland, labourer, of Runcorn, was charged with being helplessly drunk in Moughland's- lane.—P.C. Bancroft deposed to discovering hien there on the 6:h of August in the condition described:—Super- intendent Pearson stated that the defendant whe was locked up bad refused to get bail and bad consequently been detained a couple:of days:—The Bench in considera- tion of that fast liberated the man on payment of 2s 61 fine.
HALTON WESLEYAN ANNUAL SCHOOL TREAT.

The annual treat of the Halton Trinity Wesleyan Sun, day School took place on Monday last, The scholars as.Jembled at :the schools at a quarter to two, and after singing and prayer, formed its procession and marched to Duke's field, led by Mr. William Nixon. All kinds of games were indulged in until about 4 o'clock, when the children re-assembled at the schools and partook of an excellent tea. The attendance was so large, however, that it was necessary to have three sittings to accommo- date the whole. After tea the field was again repaired to and amusements kept alive until 8.30. Re-255e1nb1ing in front of the chapel at that hour, the children were each presented with a bag of nuts or sweets. A pleasant feature of the treat was that this year a large numb'r of the elder scholars had turned up. The officers present were :—Messrs James Looker, J B Clarke, W Rowe, (superintendents), W Astbury and Peter Rowlinson, (secretaries).—At the tea tables a pleasant reference was made to the Rev J R Clifton, who is leaving the Run- corn Circuit.
GOOD News FOR RUNCORN.—A FUELTILEII SIGN OF PROSPERITT•

The announcemeat made some time age in the columns of the " Examiner" that a new industry was about to commence at the Old Gas Works near the Spinets is now amply verified. We are informed semi- officially that Messrs. George A. Watson and Company, brokers, Szc., Liverpool, completed negotiations with Mr. J. R. Frith,secretary and manager of Runcorn Gas Com- pany, for the leasing of the eld gas works off Bridge- street, which have been idle for five years. The lease will contain a purchase clause centaining terms agree- able to both parties: Messrs. Watson have acquired the works for a new company which is being formed fee this manufacture of quicksilver, and it is understood that most of the capital is being subscribed in Glasgow. The process it is intended to work is te extract quicksilver from Spanish ere, for which the company have acquired valuable mining rights in Spain. The gasworks will have to undergo considerahle alteration in order to render them suitable for the new industry. They are well situated on the banks of the Bridgewater Canal,and the raw material and the manufactured article can be imported and exported with ease. The Castner Kellner Chemical Company, whose works are in the district, employ a large quantity of quicksilver in their electroly- tical process of manufacturing alkali. _
RUNCORN CADETS OF TEMPERANCE.-GDIDE OF YOUTH
SECTION.

An interesting meeting of the above Order was held on Saturday evening in the Greenway-road Sch. )1, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Cooke. The Chair- man, in opening the proceedings, said he had a pleasant task to perform. Six months ago two of their friends, Messrs. Edward Key, jun., and George Holt, offered two prizes for those members who introduced the largest number cf members to their section. The first prize was won by Leonard Whyte. It consisted of a beautifully-bound book, entitled "Swiss Family Robinson." The second prize was won by Leonard Ellison, and consisted of a copy of " Rebin- son Crusoe," well bound, with gilt edges. The Chairman said he was sorry there had not been more competitors, and urged those present to do more for the cause in the future. He reminded them that next Saturday they were having their demenstration,aed they intended to have a lifeboat in the procession.—Mr. Edward Key, sea., proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Cooke for presiding, and made a few encouraging re- marks to the 5 °wig people. He appealed te them to work :nore enthusiastically for the temperance cause.— Mr. Dank' Bisbrown, in seconding the resolution, re- minded the boys that theirs was a twofold pledge— against drink and against tobacco. He hoped that right through life they would set their faces against this bad nahit. He regarded it as a waste of money arid as not being conducive to health.—The vote of thanks was carried unanimously. RUNCORN FREEMASONS' PICNIC.

The annual install4tion picnic in connection with the Elleimere Lodge (753) of Ancient, Free, and Accepted Masons was held on Thursday, the destination this year being Bakewoll, Derbyshire. The party left Widnes about 8.20 a.m., and, after a journey through some of the most picturesque scenery in Cheshire and Derbyshire Bikowell was reaoned about Qlevela o'clock. Alsout an hour was spent in a stroll around the town, by the end of which time dinner was ready at the Castle Hotel. Here a splendid repast was served, the catering being ng everythi that could he desired. At two o'clock convey- ances were in attendance to convey the visitors to Chats- worth, the'seat of the Duke of Devonshire, and Had- don Hall. These were reached after a most enjoyable drive, and the visit to both places, as also to Chatsworth Church, proved to be full of interest. At the church the party viewed the grave of the late Lard Frederick Charles Cavendish. Tho visitors returned to the Castle Hotel, Bikewell, and partook of tea, and the return journey was commenced at eight o'clock, arriving at Widnes 9.50 p.m. The day was in every respect favour- able to the proceedings, and the picnic was conceded to be one of the most successful ever held. Amlug those present were :—Messrs H Branch, W.M. ; E Newton, S.W. ; E C Hicks, J.W. ; W R Wass, P.P.G., D.D. of C., P.M., treasurer; T H Annett, P.P.G.T., P.M., secretary ; U W Handley, J.D. ; J Salkeld, P.M. ; W Hankinson, P.M. ; S Taylor, W Kirkham, J hudor, J Collier ; Mrs Branch, Miss Branch, Mrs Hicks, NI rs Annett, Miss E Annett, Miss A Abel, Miss C Abel, Miss Hankinson, and others.

DEPARTURE OF TUE REV. R. J. CLIFTOW.I Last Sunday the Rev. R. J. Clifton preached his fare- well sermon in St. Paul's Wesleyan Church, Runcorn. Basing his remarks on Mark vi. 31, the rev, gentleman said ell the three-years system Wesleyan ministers took up their work in one place only to drop it again, and proceed to other spheres and pastures new. God, how- ever, wont with them. He will remembered looking round on the congregation three years ago. Yet he felt no fear, for he had unbounded confidence in the loyalty and the love of the Methodist Church. When it was his lot to come among them, he came knowing that the care of God would still be with him. His sermons were, psrhaps, sometimes miserably poor, but he never went out of the pulpit without saying sharper things CO himself than ever anyone else could have uttered. Sometimes a poor sermon was the means of blessing some poor brother. The pews made their contribution towards every sermon. Many of the persons present had helped to make his preaching a work of love, and he thanked them ter it. He always gave them of his best though even that was often poor. He believed in the church to which he belonged, and did not mean to run away from it. They should be true to the church where they had received so many blessings. They should train their children in the old Methodist principles. He never looked down on the congregation without thinking of one fine old man, and Chao were many others who had done good work in the old days. H ewished more would follow in the footsteps of those who had followed their Master so well. He trusted the young fellows of Bruns- wick and St. Paul's would do better work than their fathers had done. The service was closed by the choir singing the anthem, " God be With you till we meet again."

div.head: ASSA.IILTING AN OLD WOUAN AT
div.p: ASSA.IILTING AN OLD WOUAN AT
WESTON.
KICKING AND THREATENING TO KILL.

An extraordinary case came before the Runcorn magistrates on Saturday when Mr. F. Wiswall presided, and Mr. F. J. Norman also sat.—Michael Costello was charged en warrant with assaulting Margaret McMahen. at Weston, on the 24th July. Prosecutrix stated that she lived in Riley's-row, Wes- ton. She was a widow and was in her 78th year. For five years she kept the reading room at Weston. On the 24th July the met with the prisoner's wife in a neigh- bour's house. The prisoner said to witness "Do you know this person ?" (meaning prisoner's wife), and witness replied " No." She said " It's Mrs. Costello," and the woman gOt up and shock hands with witness. Witness said" 'don't know you," whereupon Mrs. Costello said "You did me many a good turn when I was in Weston before by lending me a shilling." Witness replied "That's past and over." Mrs. Costello subsequently came into witness's house. She looked very much upset and said "I have only come here a day or two ago; lam going to keep a couple of lodgers." The woman went out, but returned shortly afterwards. She put half a sovereign and a two-shilling piece on the table, and said to witness "Take that, for I have plenty of money. I got it with that fire that was in St. Helens." She gave witness to understani she had been hurt, and showed her her head. Witness asked "What are you giving me this for? I don't want it." Mrs. Costello left the house and witness put the money in the cupboard. Prisoner's wife returned in a short time, and witness had on the table a clock she was going to raffle to raise money for a pair of boots. Prisoner's wife said "All these things (the furniture) are mine." Witness said "There's nothing here but what belongs to me. After I'm dead and gone I don't know who'll get them. Perhaps the parish will get them." The woman then attacked witness. She kicked her and knocked her down, and the prisoner came into the house and assisted her. He struck witness with the pek.r (produce 1) on the wrist ani caused a wound. His wife called her an Orangewoman, and " kicked her un- der the dresser and under the table as long as she could." She also told the prisoner to kick her until be killed her. Alter the assault the prisener and his wife slept in the house, on the room floor, aad witness slept in another little room. The prisoner and his wife took half-a- gallon of neer upstairs ; she found the bottle after they had cleared off. After the assault her head was all cut and battered, and she had to be bandaged up. In con- sequence of her ill-treatment she was in bed for nearly a sv.ek.—ln reply Co the prisoner, witness denied that she signfel a paper, selling the furniture to the prisoner. Be hit her with the poker that lay near the kitchen fire. He also kicked her under the dresser, and then threw the poker after her. The prisoner never lodged with her nor his wife either.—Prisoner : I never touched you that night with the poker. I might give you a shove.— Priooner toll the Bench that prosecutrix fell downstairs, but she denied it.

Margaret Casey, Riley's-row, Weston, stated that she was the grand-daughter of the prosecutrix. On Monday th. 24th July, about 6.30 p.m., she saw the prisoner taki hold of the nrosecu •rix by the back of the shoulder and throw her on the floor. Prior to this the prosecu- trix had been telling prisoner and his wife to go out; they had no business there. Prisoner said he would not ge •. his wife had bought all the furniture, and it was his house. He then hicked the prosecutrix, and his wife followed his example. The wife had no shoes OR. The prisoner picked the prosecutrix several times. Witness did not see toe poker used, she went for P.C. Wylie, the village constable. The prisoner had his boots on. Witness did not see him strike the last witne-s with the poker. When witness returned the clock was in the yard, and her grandmottAr had been taken into a neighbour's house Her head was " allof a jelly." Prosecutrix had been ill ever since the assault was committed.

Margaret Kilgrass, married woman, living in Riley's- row, stated that about seven o'clock on the night of the 24th July she beard a row outside and went to the door. She saw the neighbours round Mrs. McMahen's door, and on going there she heard the old woman screaming for mercy. The prosecutes lay across the hearth and she was saying to the prisoner "You have staved my ribs in, you brute." The prisoner was standing over her, but he did not kick her while witness was present. Witness called out to him "don't ' kill the poor old woman." The prisoner had his foot raised as if to kick the prosecutrix. He seemed to be very fresh in drink. His wife sat in a corner laughing. She was quite drunk, and calling the prose- cutes foul names. The proaecutrix tried to get posses- sion of the clack, and prisoner gave her a shove and sent her a couple of yards, causing her to fall. Witness said" Oh my, she's dead." The old woman was brought into witness's house, and it was then found that she was hurt very much about the head. One eye was '6 knocked up," and there were lumps all over her head. The prosecutes was perfectly sober when witness went there. The prisoner and his wife had been having beer in another neighbour's house.—Prisoner : She stuck to my half-sovereign whether she was sober or not. Prisoner said.the old woman fell and be took her up- stairs. She was drunk and he (prisoner) was drunk. His head had not been right since he was at the ex- plosion._ -__ _ _

P. C. Wylie stated that he apprehended the prisoner at Ashton-in-Maherfield on Friday. When charged with the offence the prisoner said "We were all drunk. Mrs. McMahon fell downstairs." The prosecutrix had a black lump behind her right ear. There were also black lumps OR her head and bruises on her arms.
The Chairman (to the prisoner) : We consider the case proved against you, and you will have a month, with hard labour.

div.head: FRODSHAM ROADMA.N DEFENDS HIMSELF WITH HIS BRUSH.
div.p: A FRODSHAM ROADMA.N DEFENDS HIMSELF WITH HIS BRUSH.

Messrs. A. Thomas and John Ockleston were the magistrates whe sat at the Frodsham Occasional Court, on Wednesday. when Henry Faulkner, of Overton, Frodsham,was brought up in custody charged with bo• in drunk and disorderly, and also with threatening John Corker, readinan in the employ of the Cheshire County Council, on Tuesday, 6th August. Prisoner pleaded guilty to both offences. John Corker, said he was a roadman, in the employ of the Cheshire County Council. On Tuesday he was follow- ing his occupation on Chester Main-road, some time in the morning, when the prisoner came and asked him whether he had any money. Witness replied " No." Prisoner then became violent, and threatened to knock his head off if he would not give him money. Witness again refused, and prisoner returned to him in a threat ening attitude. Corker said he could. not stand,that and "up's with his brush and knocks ppsoner over." This was the second occasion upon which Corker had been annoyed by the man. Police Constable Dickins testified to apprehending the prisoner who was in a very drunken condition. He swore and used bad language. The Bench imposed a flue of 20s. including cost or one month in default for being drunk ; and for threatening Corker, prisoner was bound over in his own recognis- ances of £5 to keep the peace for six months.—The Chairman added that should Faulkner come before them again be would be most severely dealt with indeed.

div.head: PROROGATION OF PARLIA.MENT.
div.p: PROROGATION OF PARLIA.MENT.

The fourth session of the 14th Parliament of Queen Victoria was brought to a close at half-past two o'clock ,on Wednesday afternoon. The QIIREN'S Speech, which I was read by the LORD CHANCELLOR with the cuatornary ceremony, contained Hale of interest, with the excep• ton of an important allusion to the Transvaal troub7 - It opened with a reference to the conclusion of the Peace Conference, which, "although the result of its delibera- tions had not fully eorrespeaded with the lofty aims which it was summoned to accomplish, had mot with a , considerable measure of success. The Convention with France as to the valey of the Nile, and the agreement with tßussia with respect to railway enterprise in China, were next briefly touched upon. The reference to the Transvaal difficulty coatainei the following notable passage—" The position of my sub- jects in the Soutil African Republic is inconsistent with the promises of equal treatment on which ray grant of internal independence to that Republic was founded,and the unrest caused thereby is a constant source of danger to the peace and prosperity of my dominions in South Africa." The negotiations with the South African Re- public were stated to be still proceeding. The Speech concluded with references to the condition of India. the 'Niger purchase, the London Government Act, and other measures which have received the Royal assent. In the House of Commons, Mr. Chamberlain was in duced by a pro-Boer speech from Mr. T. P. O'Connor once more to express the determination of the &were- ment to put an end to the Uitlanders* grievance:. British predominance in South Africa, he said, was men- aced by the refusal of the Republic to redress these grievances, which had been brought to its notice in the most moderate language by t'ee suvrain Power. This was a state of things which could not be tolerated, and, as he had said before, the Government had 'pat their hands to the plough and would not turn back. At ten minutes past two "Black Rod" was announced, and General Sir Miami. BIDDEILPH. the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, appeared at the bar, and, advancing to the table, anuminced in the visual form that the Lords, who were outherised by virtue of her Majesty's Commission to declare the Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Rouses and to pro. rogue Parliament, desired the iesnaediate attendance of that honourable House in the Boise of Peers to hear the somilinlia read.

As soon as the reernhcrs had taken their seats, the right honourable gentleman rose, and, in accordance with the usual practice, read the Qiteen's Speech. The members then passed the table in single Me, each shak- ing hands with the Speaker:

div.head: WAR KIN GTON.
div.p: WAR KIN GTON.
THE BANE NOLIDAY.

Bank Holiday opened rather dull but the weather appeared brighter towards dinner time and though occasionally promising rain it fortunately held off. Large numbers of people left the town going to the usual resorts and the London and North-Western Railway Company and the Cheshire Lines Committee had their organizing powers well tested. This increase in the day's traffic, so far as the London and North-Western Railway are con- cerned, was doubtless due to the suspension ot the week-end excursion tickets. The company will have to admit a heavy loss to is finances, and the experiment is not likely ta be repeated. The other companies reaped the reward, and had a record week-end. In town there was the attraction of the Football Sports, which were well patronised. The theatres were also well attended. At night the principal :streets of the town were crowded with returning excursionists. Some ngures witk regard to the bookings at the Central Station will not be uninteresting:—Liverpool and New Brighton 3,000, Manchester 1000, Southport 1,500, Bell Vue 200, Matlock and district 250, Isle of Man 900, North Wales Steamboat 200. Monday was con- sidered to have been the busiest day ever ex- perienced at the Cheshire Lines Station. SECOND HAND CYCLES, LARGE QUANTITY for ALE or HIR.I3.—J, S. GARLAND, Bridge-street. div.head: CONCERT _ AND DANCE AT WHITLEY.
div.p: CONCERT _ AND DANCE AT WHITLEY.

A concert and dance was 1-Ce in—&-';;;sembly Rooms, Grimsolitch Mill, on Monday evening, the artistes for the clncert giving every satisfaction. Mr. W Hughes sang "One of the Light Brigade" in a very creditable manner. Mr. Harry Cattail again created roars of laughter with his merry little family of dolls. Mr. S Aukland was loudly applauded for his performances on the mandoline, Japanese fiddle, concertina, and tubeph one ; whilst Mr. W W Whittle, the Lancashire favourite humorist and character comedian, received well-merited encores and kept the house in roars of laughter, with his hurnourous songs, "The Shipwrecked Captain" and "The Railway Guard." He also gave an extra turn for Mr. Sycl. Griffith, who was indisposed. Mr. J T Barton, of Warringtom, proved a very efficient accompanist. Dancing was afterwards kept up till after 2 a.m , everyone appearing to have thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

PROFESSOR of English Literature (to modern young man)—" How would you punctuate this sentence, 'The beautiful girl for such she was rode out into the night on her bicycle?'" Student—" I think, Professor, Iwould make a dash after the beautiful girl." " WHY don't you hold up your head as I do :' " inquired a lawyer of a small farmer. "Squire," replied the farmer, " look at that field of wheat. All the valuable heads hang down like mine, while those that have nothing in them stand upright like yours." ONCE BITTEN TWICE SHY.—Owner: So you think you have a customer for my farm? Agent : I've been negotiating with a man who says he used to own one. Owner: Don't have anything to do with him. He's a fraud. No one who ever owned a farm would want to buy another.

THERE'S A REMEDY FOR EVERYTHING, —A miner informed his landlord that through a water-pipe having burst at the end of the house his hens had all been drowned. Landlord: "When did this happen?" Miner: "Last night, and I want to know what lam going to do." Landlord: "Keep ducks in future."

PAVING THE WAY. —Mr. Sponger: " Wifey, what date is this ? " Mrs. Sponger : "The fifth. Why do you ask?" Mr. Sponger: "I am writing to Uncle Hiram, in Scroogeville, asking why he and the family didn't come down and see us during the winter."

HUSBAND: "Confound the razor." Wife: "What's the matter now? You're dreadfully cross- tempered." Husband: "The razor is so abomin- ably dull ! " Wife: " Dull ? Why, I ripped up an old skirt with it yesterday, and it cut beautifully !”

MRS. SCRIBBLES: "I believe the butcher is knocking at the door with his bill, Ferdinand." Scribbles: "Tell him I am sorry, but I've just paid the rent, and am short." Mrs. Scribbles: "But it may be the landlord, Ferdy." Scribbles: "Well, then, tell him I'm sorry, but I've just paid the butcher, and am short ."

"WHAT A COO ! "—A number of Sir Wilfrid Lawson's tenants were being entertained one day at dinner. There were plenty of aerated waters and milk for such as liked them, but nothing stronger. One of the farmers, who knew by ex- perience what to expect, had provided himself with a flask of rum, and, unknown to a brother farmer who sat next to him, he poured a generous Quantity into the glass of milk which his neighbour had elected to drink. In due time the unsuspect- ing farmer put the glass to his lips, and seemed to enjoy it so that he never stopped till he had finished it; then he turned to his friend and re. marked: " Hech ! man Thomas, what a coo I" "REPRINTED BY REQUEST."—SeveraI years ago, when the editor of a Chicago daily was running a country weekly down in Indiana, he had occasion to go to the capital on the day before the regular weekly issue, Calling in the foreman, he said: "Jim, I'll have to let you get out the paper to- morrow, as I'm going away. There is plenty of matter in type now, so all you'll have to do is to make up the formes and go the press. If you should need any more stuff you may run the long editorial on the tariff which I printed last week and preface it with the words Reprinted by re- quest." Two days later the editor returned to find everything moving along nicely and the fore. man flushed with the success of his experience as editor pro. tern. "Everything went like clock- work, sir," he said. "It was as easy as falling off a log. I had to use your editorial again, though, to fill up." And he proudly displayed a paper dwhich had in the middle of the first page the old, familiar editorial, with the explanation in black- faced type: "Printed again by the request of the editor."
