div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
FRIDkIr.- Before the Mayor (in the chair), and Alderman

Boberts. ASSAITLT ON A LITTLE Ginr,.—Thomas Cotton, labourer, 39, Morris-yard, Church-street, was charged with committing an assault on Ellen Smith on the 28th July.—Defendant pleaded not guilty. —The Chief Constable said the charge had been reduced from one of inch scent assault to common assault, to enable the magistrates to deal with it. The complainant who was twelve years of age, and daughter of William Smith, brass moulder, Marsh-street, gave evidence of the assault which took place in Marshouse lane —Two brothers of the complainant, both youeg boys. gave corroborative evidence, and the bench committed prisoner to prison for three months' hard labour. TRESPASSING ON THE RAILWAY.—Thomas Taylor. 12, Sparling-street, William Sheratt. 10. York-street, James Kay, 26, New-rcad, Robert Critchley, 27, Krauts ford-road, and John Henry Hollowell. 32, New-road. were all summoned for trespassing on the London and North Western Railway on the 19th JAy.—Mr. Foam, who appeared to prosecute said they were endeavouring to stop this practice.—Constable Metcalfe said on the dav in question (Sunday). between two and 3 o'clock he was on duty in plain clothes with Constable Bennett at the top of St. Mary's-street. They saw the five defendants along with six more young men in a field belong- ing to the Warrington Brick and Tile Company playing pitch and toss. The five defendants ran away as soon as they saw them (the officers) —Constable Bennett corroborated,and the defendants were fined ss, each including costs. ASSAULT.—Henty Taylor, 3, Morris-court was charged with assaulting Ellen Mee, who lived at the same address,on the 21st July.—Complainant said she was washing when de- fendant came up to her and struck her.—Dcfendant said he only gave her a push with one of his hands.—He was fined 5s and costs or seven days. NOT THRoUGE COLD BUT FEAR —James Blunett was charged with using threats towards Martin Farrington on the 29th July.—Bo!h reside in Piernoint-street—Complain- ant stated defendant came up to him and shook his fist in his face saying, 'what I can't do with this I'll do with a b—knife." —Three or four witnesses corroborated.- -Asked by the Magisarates' Clerk whether he was suffering through this threat complainant replied : " I've been shiver- ing all this week."—The defendant denied the threat and called two witnesses but the magistrates bound him over and ordered hint to pay Cat costs. MORE THREATS.—MichaeI Corless, 3, Aikin-street, was also charged with using threats towards Elizabeth Lewis, 80, Priestley-street, on the 29th July.—Cemplainant gave evi- dence ol the threats and the defends nt was bound over and ordered to pay the costs (ss). "WANTED SOMEWHERE To SLEEP."—Thomas Fahey, tramp, was charged that being a person of suspicious &er- ecter, he was found loitlring in Thelwall-lane that morning with intent to commit a felony.—P.C. Plumb said he was on duty in Thelwall-lane and heard a dog barking for about an ' heur, At ten minutes to one he saw the prisoner crossing from side to side examining windows and doors. He stopped the man and asked him what he was doing. Prisoner replied that he was looking for a place t) get in to sleep.—Tne Chief Constable said there had been something like a scare in Thelwall-lane lately through various burglaries that had occurred there.—Prisoner was commi.ted for seven days. THREE MONTHS FOR NEGLECT.—lisitac Bickley, 9, Roger- street, was charged with neglecting his two children, Mary Ellen and Elizabeth, to the danger of their health.—Mr. Browne, who appeared to prosecute for the N.S.P.C.O, said the defendant was a widower ard was getting 35s per week. He was in regular work and would get no one to look after the children. In this case there had been eightdifferent visits by the Inspector to the house a companied by the police and on one occasion by Dr. Bowden.—Evidence was given by the Inspector, police constables and Dr. Bowden which disclosed a shocking state of affairs the children being poorly clad and covered with vermin. Dr. Bowden stated that the house in which they lived was not fit for human habitation.—The Bench committed defendant for ,three months with hard labour. ANo rHER CHANCE.—Martha Potter, 53, Watkin-street, was also summoned by the Society for neglecting her five chil- dren.—Defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr Brown said in this case they had given the defendant ten opportunities. They had not summoned the husband as he was not to blame. The husband gave defendant 20s per week and bought the children's clothes and one of the children was also bringing in a few shillings a week. Mr Browne proceeded to give de- tails of the visits paid to the defendants house which disclosed a disgusting state of life but the magistrates without going into the evidence decided to give the woman another chance and adjourned the case. SATURDAT.—Betere Me_sars, S. Ohandley (in the chair) and
R. T. Fakelough:

AN UNHAPPY MARBLED LlFE.—JanTes Astley, 123, Orford- lane was charged with assaulting his wife, Alice Astley on the 13th July.—He pleaded guilty.—Complainant said de- fendant came home about dinner time on the 13th July, and without any cause whatever threw his coat, the pockets of which contained some tools, at her, hitting her in the face. On the previous day he threw a shovel at her. He was under the intlaence of drink at the time and he always ill-used her when he ad had drink. She was afraid of him,and dreaded him coming in the house. He had b: an away from home for about two weeks, and had given her no mcney. She had five children to keep —The Clerk stated that defend ant should have appeared on July 28th and also on Friday, ween a warrant was issued for his arrest.—The Chief Con- stable said he knew the man very well. He used to be a very steady man.—He had said that he wanted a seearation himself.—The Caairman (to complainant) Haven't you any hopes of a reform Promise to live with him again, and we saul bind him over. Complainant : He has told people that he wanted a separa- tion order, and would give me El per week.—The Chief Constable remarked that detendent was ayery ob:dinate man. He had been asked to come to some agreement with his wife, but he refused. He was a man with a very violent temper. He had been before the Court twice previously.—The Chair- man said they would take the case as an aggravated assault, and tine defendant lOs including costs. They would also grant a separation order, the wile to receive £1 per week. A TIMELY ARREST.—William Curley was charged with having been drunk and disorde.ly in Buttermarket-street, on Friday night.—He pleaded guilty.—P.C. F. Monks said he saw the prisoner thrown out of a public-house, and he became very disorderly. On seeing witness he said he did not care for the whole of the police force ; he could do away with the lot.—The Cnief Constable : So you brought him d.,wn to the Police Station to prevent our extinction. (Laughter.) Prisoner has a very bad record, having been before thee court many times previously, mainly for assault.—He was com- mitted to prison for 14 days with hard labour. MONDAY.—l3efore the Mayor, Mr. Alderman Wright (chair man), Mr. F. Monks, Alderman B ackhurat and Mr. S. Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—EIIen Connor (62nd appear- ance) end Mary Brown (23rd appearance) were charged with being drunk and disord rly in Ship-yard on Saturday even- ne.—P.C. Turner proved the case, and the prisoners were committed to prison for one month's hard labour.—James &lahoney, of Foundry-street, for a similar offence in Wilson Patten street, was fined ss, including costs, and Elizibeth Evans, for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket- street, at 11.3) on Saturday evening was fined a like amount. —Margaret Utley, for drunkenness and indecent behaviour In Frughall-lane on Saturday midnight was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days imprisonment. INDECENT BEHAVlOUlL—klargaret McLoughlin, of Ship Yard, was committed to prison for one month on the evid- ence of P.C. Turner, for her indecent, behaviour in Ship Yard on Saturday evening. DAMAGE To CiROwING CRoM—Sarali Hunt and Elizabeth Beckley were charged under a warrant with committing wilful damage to a growing field In the occupation of James Newton and doing damag3 to the ezt na of one shilling.—The Chief Constable stated that the priseners were served with summonses but

A nOUGH Musnamp.—Jantes Whittaker, 3, Providence- place was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Longford- street on the 3 th July.—Mr. H. Taylor, Pollee Court Missionary, said he was arousal from sleep about half past eleven on the Sunday night in question by hearing some- one shouting and swearing outside his house Witness got up and on 'ooking through the window saw the defendant beating a young woman very severely. fle asked him to desist and as he would not witness hid the woman be would comedown. When he get down into the street the defend• ant had dragged the woman who was his jwife, into Orford- lane where be was kicking at her. Defendant used very abusive language to him. P.C. Plumb arrived en the scene and took them home.—Fined lOs and eosts or 14 days.

MEELCE OF TEE PE&CE.--SErah Leonardy and James Leonardy, mother and son, residing lu Silyer-square, were charged with carnmitaing a brea3h of the peace by being disorderly in Silver-square on the 30th July,—Sarah Leonardy only appeared and was bound over and orderel to pay the nests.

Dauttz P.( CiraTlGE.—John Deakin, 35. Winwick-road,was chargad with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart at 8-30 the previous night in linntsford-road.—P.C.lCorcoran said he saw the defendant corning from the direction of the swing bridge driving at a fearfel rate. • mat fell out of the cart and later the cart spilled and the other two nen and the defendant fell oat. They had not waited to pick the man np who first fell ont.—George Chappell. Inspector Phillips and John Howard, smith Wash-lane. a'eo gave evidence and defendant was fined 10s and costs (21 2s 6d) or 14 days. WEDNESDAT.—Before Alderman Fainlough (in the chair)

SILVER-SQUARE AGAlN.—James Leonardy, Silver-square was charged on a warrant with eommittlng a breach of the peace by being disorderly in Silver-square on July 30th.— P.O. Baxendale said he was in Silver-street at a quarter to three on Sunday morning, 30th July. when he heard a dis- turbance in Silver-square. He proceeded there and saw defendant and others singing and dancing. He put the de- fendant in his house. but he came out again and continued his disordeely conduct. He put him in a second time, and defendant then picked up a bottle and attempted to assault him.—The Chief Constable stated that defendant had been before the Court 21 times in a very short space of time.— Defendant was ordered to pey the costs and was bound over to keep the peace for six months. SHE CAME TO BE TRIED BY GENTLEMEN.—Annie Walsh, no settled abode, was charged with having been drunk in Friars'-green at five minutes.past one the same morning.— P.S. Evans proved the ease. —The Chief Constable stated that the defendant had been several times before the magistrates in other towns.—Defenthant said that she had come there to be tried by gentlemen. not by the Chief Constable,—She was fined lOs and costs (13s 6,1). A CORNERMIN SENT TO GAOL.—James Hopkins, a well- known character, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, at 7 20 on Tuesday night, and also with having assaulted P.C. Clough whil t in the execution of his duty.—Prisoner denied the assault.—P.C. Clough said he saw the defendant in Horsemarket-street. He was very drunk. He noticed him stopping men, and ask- ing them for four pence for a night's lodging. When they refused he used bad language. Witness took him up Town- hill, but became back again. He again used very bad language and witness Was obliged to teke him into custody. Prisoner then became very violent, and kicked witness on the back. P.C. Cooper appeared on the scene, and they took prisoner to the Police Station.—P C. Cooper gave corroborative evidence.—The Chief Constable said that was prisoner's 26th appearance. Prisoner and his brother, who was in gaol, were perfect street corner pests. He had pre- viously been sent to gaol for three months for assaulting the police.—Prisoner was fined 5a for having been drunk and disorderly and one month'a imprisonment with bard labour for the assault.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie (chairman), Col. Wood, C.B. F Borron. and S. 6. Brown. LlCENSlNG.—Elizabeth Ridyard applied for the transfer of the license of a beer house in Heath-street, Golborne, from her late husband Peter Ri4yard.—Granted.—Temporary authority to sell at the Royal Oak, Golborne, was granted to Joseph Wright in place of William Glover.—John Forster was granted temporary authority to sell at an out beer house In High-street, Golborne. in place of John Parr. ALTERATIONS To A. BEERHOUSE.—Mr. A. Browne submitted plans of intended alterations to the haerhouse, Sign i'th Cellars, Golborne, and applied f, r permission. The police had no objection to the plans which had been passed ty the local authority.—The magistrates gt anted the application. DRUNEENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for being drunk and disorderly :—Richard Wilkinson. 25th July 2e 6d and costs 1 Job Hilton. 29th July, 2a 6d and costs ; William Scott. 29th July, 28 6d and costs; Joseph Thorpe , 22nd July. 2s 61 and costa ; Jahn Dunn,22nd July, 2s 6d and costs; Thomas Travis. 22nd July (19th appearance), 50 and costs ; James Noon, 23rd July, 58 and costs ; John Foy, 26th July, 5s and costs ; Michael Joyce, sth August (14th appear- &nee), 20s and costs ; and Patrick McGrait and Robert Abbott 9th August. 2s 6d and costs each.—Fines were imposed on the following for being drunk --Benjamin Concannon, sth Angust, 5s and costs ; Gerald Farrell, sth August. 2s 6d and costs ; and Patrick Mollett, 22nd July, 28 6d and costs. OTHER OFFENCES.—James Greaves, for driving without a light on the 26th July at Haydock, was fined 3s 6d.— William Winstanley, Edward Jones, Arthur Bolton, and Thomas Dover, all Golborne lads, were summoned for doing damage to oats the property of Charles Jenkinson.—Bolton did not appear, and tbe other defendants pleaded guilty, , —P.O. Wilde proved the case.—Mr. Jenkinson said the damage amounted to jabout 28 each--The defendants said they had been bathing.—Defendants were ordered to pay the damage, 28 each and coats. CONFLICTING EvIDENCE.—Alfred Unsworth was charged with assaulting Johulloyers on the 3rd August at Burton- wood.—John Moyers said the defendant lodged with him and he (complainant) told him to go away. Defendant refused, threw him o if hls chair into a corner of the room, and said he woule choke him.—Defendant admit- ted havin_, th •iwn nomplainant off his chair.—Mary Alice Moyers, wife of complainant, said her husband struck the defendant in the month before Unsworth threw him off the chair.—Questioned by the Magistrates' Clerk (Mr Henry Greenall) witness said she had had bothers with her husband ever einee they had been married. He had deserted her once.—Complainant denied striking defendant first.—A young woman who said she was sister to complainant, said that Unsworth came to her mother's house and asked to see her brother. He said he wanted to be friends. Witness asked him what about and defendant replied " the bother." She asked him what business he had to throw her brother off his chair and what business he had to go walking with her brother's wife. Witness then made an allegation againist defendant which Mr. Greenall said she had no right to say witt:eut proof.—Defendant, questioned, said he went to see John Moyers "about him scandalizing his name up and down the place."—Samuel tones said he saw the bother. Defendant started it by striking complainant. But Boyers never was off his chair whilst he was in the house.—The beach dismissed the case

On Monday afternoon the Sunday school scholars of the above chapel had their annual treat in a field in Westy-lane, kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Thomas Ford. The afternoon was pleasantly spent, in various games and sports. At four o'clock tea was served in the Teutperance Ball, when abont 200 at down. After tea an adjournment was again made to the field, where the scholars enjoyed them- selves until dusk.
Old Established, Honest Dealers, SCALES AND SONS, 83, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. A LOCAL FIRM'S JUBILEE.

The celebration of the 50th anniversary of the commencement of the business of Messrs Thomas Allen and Sons, of Bridge-foot, Warrington ,plumbers and painters, was an outing given to their employee to Liverpool and New Brighton. The men, with their wives, accompanied by the principals of the firm, made the journey to Liverpool by an early train. A capital knife and-fork tea was iaid for the party, numbering over 40, and the catering of Mr. Outram. who by the way will be remembered as an old Warringtonian,received full justice. After tea,Mr Barker proposed a vote of thanks to Messrs. T. Allen and Sons for their kindness and hospitality. Mr. Newell seconded the proposition, which was carried by acclamation. Mr. John Allen responded, and re- ferred to the pleasing fact that they were able to meet so many of their employes under such favour- able auspices, He considered that the relationship between employers and employed should be of such a character as to coramana mutual respect and a kindly regard for each other's welfare. Each man was the recipient of a booklet, reprinted from a " Descriptive accout of Warrington (illustrated) of to-day." which contains an account of the career of the firm.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
POLICK CASE.
At the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J. Kent was charged with being drunk at Earlestown on Friday night and was fined 2s. 6d. and Mts. EAXLESTOWN MISSION.

On Monday the scholars of the Sunday school connected with the above Mission had their annual treat. There was no procession but about 250 scholars and teachers assembled at tie grand stand at Newton race course,whigh had been kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Pardey,aud whilst the child- ran enjoyed themselves in various ways, a cricket match was played between the married and single members, resulting in a victory for the latter. Tea partaken of in one of the rooms add was heartily enjoyed by those present. After tea racing and other games were indulged in until dusk when the company dispersed.

div.head: BANK HOLIDAY AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: BANK HOLIDAY AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

The August Bank Holiday was observed in Earlestown and Newton generally. In previous years very little notice has been taken of this popular holiday, but as this year the Vulcan Works and. Messrs. Slee and Co., have closed for the week, it has been more generally observed. The Viaduct Works closed on Monday only, and Messrs. T. and T. Vicars closed for two days. There was a large exodus of holiday makers, and the booking at the station were exceptionally heavy. The attraction at Bartenwood in connection with the Dahlia Queen festival found relaxation for many of the stay-at- horaes,but beyond this,there was nothing of interest in the town. There was an influx of visitors to Newton, and the lake was well patronised. ST. JOHN'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual treat to the scholars attending the above school took place on Saturday afternoon under favourable circumstances. The scholars met in the church at one o'clock, and after a short ser- vice and address by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, the vicar, a przcessiou was formed outside. Headed by the Earlestown band, the scholars paraded the streets of the town,the Liverpool Farm School,leac- ing the boys. in the procession there were 1032 children and 30 teachers, and on reaching the pad- dock at Newton racs course a dispersal was made. Tea was served in the grand stand, and alter full justice was done to the viands,the children enjoyed themselves in various ways whilst the elder portion indulged in dincing until 9 o'clock, when all were dismissed to their homes. A bag containing sweets, nuts, ix., was given to each scholar.

ST. PETER'S CHTJECH, NEWTON. The annual special services in aid of the day and Sunday schools connected with St. Peter's Church, Newton, took place on Sunday. At the morning service the Vicar (Rev H Ryder) preached, and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev W J Edwardes Rees,M.A., vicar of St. Thomas', Pendle- ton. Thera were large congregations at each service. In the afternoon an organ recital was given by Mr E Hulton, Middleton, M.us Doc., F.R.C.O. dm There was a large attendance, and the following pro- gramme was submitted : —organ, 'Pilgrims Chorus" (Tanuhauser) ; song, "The Heavenly .Song," Mr W Turner; organ, " Solvieg's song"; solo," lie was despised "(Messiah) Miss Annie Molyneux ; organ, " Fugue in E flat;" organ, " Berceuse in A ; solo, "Lead, kindly light," Mr W Welsh ; organ, " Zadok the Priest." Collections were made at each service in aid of the schools.

div.head: EA.RLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL,
div.p: EA.RLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL,

On Monday the teachers of the above Sunday school had their annual picnia to Dunham Massey. With several friends the party numbered 44, and out of these 19 performed the journey on bicycles, whilst the remainder chose the easier method of wagonnette. A start was made about 10 o'clock and Dunham Massey was reached about 12-30 after a most enjoyable ride, the conditions being excellent for both cycling and driving. Dinner was served soon after,arrival, after which a sojourn through the Perk filled up the time until tea. Some of the party paid a visit to the Bowden Wesleyan Chapel, to ill- sptct the stained window, and others viewed the Bowden Church. After partaking of tea, a start was made for home about 6 o'clock, Earlestown being reached about 9. The arrangements were in the hands of Mr. T. Parr, and the outing was voted a most enjoyable one.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
FORDICOSIING LIBERAL MEBTING.

Lord Tweedmouth, who has been president of the St. Helens Liberal Association for several years, has prom- ised to pay a second visit to the town and address a Liberal demonstration on Thursday, November lfith next. It is expected that Mr. Harrep, of Manchester, the prospective Liberal candidate for the borough, and one of the most prominent Irish members will also ad- dress the meeting.

div.head: STRANGE CASE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: STRANGE CASE AT ST. HELENS.

At St. Helens Court, on Tuesday, a tramping shoc- maker named George Young, who is said to belong to Bristol, was charged with being drunk on Monday. Chief Constable Wood said Young was not present in Court, for the reason that he was now in hospital. At half past eleven the previous night he was found by Police-constable Morrison lying in an entry off Liver- pool-road. He appeared to be drunk, but the constable found he was unconscious. He tonveyod him to Arthur- street Police Station, but as he did not recover the inan was brought to the Town Hall and a doctor sent for. Drs. Reid and Masson examined him, and ordered his removal to the Providence hospital. Under the cir- cumstances he (Mr. .Wood) asked to be allowed to with- draw the summons.—The bench agreed t 3 this course. Young died later, at the Providence Hospital without recovering consciousness. He never spoke after he was found by the police.

div.head: SUPPOSED MAD Doc; AT Sr. HELENS.
div.p: SUPPOSED MAD Doc; AT Sr. HELENS.

A dog, which is strongly suspected to have suffered from rabies, was killed in St. Helens late on Sunday night. It appears that shortly after eight o'clock on Sunday night a large cross-bred retriever dog was seen in Salisbury-street, off the main thoreughtare. The animal was running about in a distressful manner, and snapped at everybody who came by. Efforts were made by various people to secure it, and the cry of" Mad dog "caused great alarm. It is rumoured that a child was bitten by the dog, and it is definitely stated that a Haydoek man, William Thomas Reid. of Cl:lurch-road, was severely bitten. The attention of Censtables Evans and Lawrence were ultimately drawn to the dog, and after some difficulty it was driven in the direction of the public abattoir, where it was killed. Mr. W. G. Dixon, the veterinary inspector for the local authority, on Monday morning made a post-mortem examination ef the carcase, and gave the opinion that it was a highly suspicious case of rabies. Mr. Dixon has forwarded part of the carcase to the Brown Institution. London, for expert examination.

div.head: BURTONWOOD DAHLIA QUEEN FESTIVAL.
div.p: BURTONWOOD DAHLIA QUEEN FESTIVAL.

IThe fifth annual festival in connection with the Coro- nation of the Dahlia Queen, took place at Burtonwood on Monday, in beautiful weather. Unlike many other outside gatherings of the kind, the Burtonwood festival since its inception has been favoured on each occasion with excellent weather, and in consequence the pro- meters have been encouraged to continue it. The prime mover in the affair is Mr. George Anders of the Bridge Inn, Burtonwood, but he has the willing assistance of the villagers in carrying out the details. The one drawback in the affair, audit is one to which we have before called attention, is that no heed whatever is paid to the time of starting the procession as advertised. The same thing happened on Monday, and instead of the procession starting at 12 30, it was nearer two o'clock before a move was made. consequently many people were tired of the long wait. The procession when it was got together was fairly lengthy, and moved off in the fallowing order :—Horse soldiers, the Dahlia Queen, (Miss Amelia Massey), in open landau drawn by a pair et horses, with maids of honour and page boys, St. Peter's Prize Band, Scotch soldiers, ex-Queen (Miss Sephton) in landau, with Maids of Honour and Page Boys, 24 Skipping Rope Dancers, Primrose Queen in cerria,ge, 24 Dahlia Pole Dancers, prettily attired ; Little 80-Peep and Boy Blue; Hospital Nurses; Britannia; Gipsies, Colliers, Italians, Red Riding Hoods, Bakers, Joiners, Szc. A number of private vehicles followed, some of which contained the smallest of the children. Tee route of the procession was via Mercer's Cottages. Wesleyan Chapel, Collins-green to a field kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Fairclough, Yew Tree Farm. Here something like 2,000 people were aeaembled who wit- nessed the proceedings in connection with the coronation of the Queen, which was performed by Miss Bessie Fair- dough of Bradley Old Hall, Burtonwood. The dancing of the Dahlia Dancers was capitally done, and reflected great credit upon Mr. J. H. Anders, their tutor: The Skipping Rope Dancers also acquitted themselves edmir- ably. The judging of the turnouts took place on the field, and resulted as follows : - -

_ Gentlemen's Turnouts :-Ist, M Pownall. Sankey; 2, T Carrigan, Buttonwood ; 3, W Austin, Earlestown. Heavy Horse and Lurry :-1, J Smith, Buttonwood ; 2, John Prescott, Buttonwood ; 3, J Faitclough, Burton- wood. The Parr band played for dancing until dusk. On Thursday, Mr. Anders entertained to tea 500 chil- dren who had taken part in the festival, and a very enjoyable afternoon was spent.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB SPORTS.

If it were needed, convincing evideuce was furnished by the" gate "on Bank Holiday that the popularity if the Warrington Football Club Sports suffers no deteriora- tion. In fact the number present on Monday was, we should say, perhaps the largest ever seen at this annual festival which has now been held for fifteen years, and this notwithstanding the fact that the weather was un- promising in the early part of the day. Happily the rain held off, securing a day of much enjoyment to the thousands gathered to witness the proceedings. Local athletes were well represented in the results, but as in previous years owing to the unbanked corners, spills were frequent in the cycle events, and though mere often than not it was the machine that suffered most, the riders: did not get off scot free. This, however,was only as it happened and was due to no particular cause. One local rider escaped serious injury by great good luck. T. Astill, was taking the bottom corner at a high speed when the machine of the rider immediately in front skidded and fell. Asti!l was unable to steer clear of the obstruction and rode ever the machine getting pitched from his saddle to within a foot of the railings. It was thought the rider had been seriously hurt but he appeared to be only suffer- ing from ElleCk when picked up. Astill did not ride again during the afternoon. It was an unfor- tunate accident, as it was considered Astill bad a good chance of winning a couple of prizes. The Warrington Borough Brass Band played an excellent selection of music the ughout the day, which was much appre- ciated. Tee following were the officials :—Clerks of the course, Messrs T Bowers and T Barnes ; starter, Mr T Waiawright ; judges. Messrs J Evans, W Dillon, T Bowers, and J T 'Thorniley ; judge of boxing competi- tion, Sergeant-Major Haigh ; committee, Messrs W Nevins, W Hewitt, J T Thorniley, F Heesora, F Moores, J T Bate, James T Bate, W Hill. T Davies, J Hackett, D Isherwoed ; handicapper, Mr W Platt ; hon.treasurer, Mr T Pemberton ; hon. secretary. Mr H Ashton ; and Mr E Pickavance represented the N.C.U.

div.head: WARRINGTON UNITED BANDS OF HOPE. GALA AND DEMONSTRATION IN VICTORIA PARK.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNITED BANDS OF HOPE. GALA AND DEMONSTRATION IN VICTORIA PARK.

Fine weather favoured the second annual de- monstration and gala promoted by the Warrington and District Band of Hope Union. The societies taking part in the procession commenced to assem- ble in front of the Town Hall about one o'clock on Bank Holiday. They carried attractiv3 banners, and some of the members of the Wycliffo Band of Hope represented various characters. One boy very successfully depicted Radjitsinnji,tbe distinguished cricketer, whilst a number of girls appeared in tie characters of flower girls, gipsies, &c. Mr. Morrall the leader of this society had generously offered prizes for the best make-up, and it was with some difficulty that the prizes could be allotted by the judge. The onerous duties of chief marshal fell upon Mr. Hutchin, and he was ably assssted by a number of officials connected with the Union. The assembling of the children was witnessed by the Mayor and Mayoress and a large number of spectators. There would be nearly '2,000 children present when the processionists were given the signal to commence the pro3ession through the town to the Victoria Park. Along the line of the route of the procession a large number of specta- tors gathered and they admired the display. The Wycliffe Society led the procession headed by the Wycliffe Band. A new banner occupied the place 'of honour. In the fcrelront walked the Rev. IE. T. Reed, Rev. J. S. Hughes, Mr. Whit- field,: Mr. . Drury, Mr. Hawthorn and others. Following the Wycliffe Society came the Legh- street Primitive Methodists, the Emmanuel and .st. James's Bands of Hope. Preceding the Buckley- street Society was the Buckley-street Brass Band, after which Came the Brick-street Mission,Golborne- street, Bank Quay Mession,Friars'-green, and Brick- street Bands of Hope. On arrival at Victoria Park sports were at once commenced, and some interest- ing events were witnessed. The dry biscuit eating match was a TIO3L laughable affair, but the keenest interest was shown in the recitation contest. There were 17 competitors and on the whole the recita- tions were admirably given. Amongst other attrac- tions were ventriloquial entertainments by Pro- fessor Wyman. The Buckley-street Band played selections of music until dusk, and many enjoyed a dance on the green sward. A cornet solo was also contributed by Mr. J. Richardson, the title of which was " The Challenge." The arrangements throughout the day were excellent, and the chil- dren thoroughly enjoyed themselves. They were provided with tea in two tents during the afternoon. 1 The following is a list of the prize winners : TEROWING TIE CRICKET BALL.-1, Allred Few ; 2 John Walls; 3, Fred Platt.

The officials upon whom the work devolved were the following :—President, Mr RIA Naylor; hon. secretaries, Messrs W Wood, and F Morrell ; treasurer, Mr E Lloyd Jones; sports committee; Messrs Hutchin, secretary. B Few, Spruce, Colley, Barker, Howard, Jolley, William Barton, Whitfield, Hodge, Ryder ; judges for recitation contest J S Hughes, Messrs Travis and Edward Jones; re- freshment committee : Miss Prince (secretary), Misses Dale, Birch, Gibson, Price, Beswick, Jones, and Birch, Messrs Dale, Ashley, Parkes, Horrocks, Sanders, Edwards, T Massey and Ryder. PUBLIC MEETING IN THE PARK.

Shortly before eight o'clock, a public meeting was hold, eir R A Naylor (who was accompanied by Miss Naylor), presiding. supporting him were the Revs E T Reed and J S Hughes, alr J W Travis, temper- ance agent, Chester, and oth3rs. After the ceremony of distributing the prizes had been gracefully discharged by Miss Naylor, the CHAIRMAN addressed the gathering. He said it was a great pleasure that they had had a fine day, and he was sure the young people would appreciate the entertainment they had had that Bank Holiday. They had many 'kind friends to thank for the suc- cess of the gathering. He believed they owed a debt of gratitude to Major Saele, who lived at the hall, for helping and making provision for the tea. (Llear,:hear.) Alluding to tee drink question, he said las only wish was that they couid get more people to join the Band of Hope and Temperance Societies. Coming along the road that evening he noticed several people intoxicated, and possibly tens of thousands of men and women, througeouc the country instead of enjoying Bank Holiday in a rational fashion, were in a similar state. There was plenty of work for Bands of Hope, and during the coming winter, every effort would be made to advance the cause of temperance. Every year they spent in the country 150 millions of peuuds in strong drink, and people who were not teetotalers were unanimous in saying that that was sadly too much. No one knew how much misery that sum represented. At the same time it was pleasing to see that the friends of temperance were trying to train the rising generation in the path they ought to walk, so that they would not be led into the drunkard's way. (Applause.) The Rev. E. T. REED then took the chair vacated by Mr. Naylor, who went to attend another meet- ing. In addressing the audience he produced a drink map of the country which had been printed by the "Christian Budget." It showed the condi- tion of the various counties of England so far as the drinking habits of the people were concerned. They would notice that the marks shown on the map were black over Northumberland, Durham and Lancashire. There was more drunkenness in these counties than in any others. There were some counties towards the:south almost entirely free from drunkenness and the fact that Lancashire was so much under the influence of strong drink should cause those who were temperance reformers to labour with all earnestness to bring about a better condition of affairs. At the present moment they were in the county of Cheshire but just across the Mersey they had to contend with a condition of things which was one of the worst in the country. He was very pleased that they had gathered to- gether under the auspices of the Band of Hope, but it was not simply through gatherings of that kind that the temperance movement spread ;it was from earnest and strenuous efforts that a re- formation in the matter of drunkenness would be brought about. (Applause.) His sympathies were entirely with the Band of Hope movement,:and he crusted that aggressive work would be undertaken during the coming winter. (Applause.) Mr. J. W. TRAVIS, of Chester, in the course of an eloquent address alluded to the hopeful condition of the Band of Hope movement, and said that if people did not drink they would never become drunkards. (Hear, hear.) It was truly said by one of the girls, when reciting, that it was not so much what they earned as what they spent. He con- tended that it required more skill and judgment to spend money wisely and well than it did for them to earn it. It was the very height of folly for a man to work from Monday morning to Saturday noon for his wages of £1 or £2 a week, and then leave six to ten shillings at the first public-house he came to. He could not understand why men so deliberately and so foolishly threw away their money upon an article which no person could in- telligently say was money value ? (Hear, hear., Not one man who bought a pint of beer g)t value for his money,and the man who continued to spend his money in drink would reap as he had sown. A man who earned XS' and spent one fourth of it at the public-house could not expect proper comfort at home beceuse it required a splendid wife to be able to keep a family out of £1 5s or .E 1 lOs per week. The annual drink bill was .E 3 16s per head in this country and if they reckoned that up they would find that the drink bill for Warrington last year was £262,000. How could it be ex- pected that they could rid the town of poverty when they put that vast Sum into the coffers of a small section of the community who did not give full value for it, and who paid the least possible wages for the longest hours ? The drink question was essentially a workingman's question. He did not wish them to blackguard every publican and brewer in Warringten, but he wished them to know that they would give up selling when they (the people) gave up buying. He appealed to them to sign the pledge and said the day would come when they would look back upon the day of their reform- ation with feelings of gladness.(Applause.) A vote of thanks was passed to Mx. Travers, on the motion of the Rev. J. S. HUGHES, seconded by the Rev. E. T. RzEre andthe meeting t-;rminated. Miss Hettie Mawsdley contributed two solos with her accustomed ability.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The return visit of the Leyland eleven to Warrington was made on Saturday. The visitors have not been beaten this season. It was not expected that Warring- ton would be able to do the trick as Leyland have a very strong eleven. Tho homestors batted first on a rather hard wicket. The game opened badly for seven wickets were lost for 53 runs owing to the capital bowling of I' Anson. Matters changed somewhat when J. W. Bibby and J Thompson were in partnership for, after getting set, they hit out with great lreedona. Changes were made in the attack but seventy runs were made in an hour. Thompson was caught low down at point, the retiring batsman having made 34 in good style. With other assistance Bibby added to the score atcl carried out his bat for 35 included in which were five boundary strokes. The Warrington innings realized 129.

The visitors did not commence too well, for Wilmct was cuight at short log by Dr. Smith. Fine batting by R. Kershaw, Hibbert, and 1' Anspn ran up the score, and the closure was applied, 191 being made at the expense of four wit;kets. iersnaw vie 74 not out, I' Anson 37, and Hibbert 26, tee visitors claiming an easy victory.

Warrington and Leyland socond elevens played at Leyland on Saturday, the visitors having a poor team. The result was inevitable. The Warringtonians were dismissed for 80 runs, of which R Pierpoint made 21, and A Picton 17. The rest of the batting was weak'. Ttie homesters played good cricket, and retired, having made 188 for five wickets. Capital batting by J Brown was responsible for 60 runs, J Barandale compiled 42 and A Caldcrbank (not out) 30, the Warrington men being decisively beaten.

On Monday a game was played at Warrington by the second eleven with North wich. W. Silcock and E. Gibson dismissed the visitors for 68. Silcook took six wickets for 17 runs. For Nerthwich A. Lyon made 28 and J. Burgess 13. Warrington, replying, made 127 runs, winning a well-deserved victory. W. M. Silcock, in good forin with the ball,was not less so with the bat, for Is credited himeelf with 52 runs. His vigorous kitting is shown by the fact that there were nine [curs included in the score. E. Pierpoint batted well for 27, and 21 (not out) was made by A. Picton.

On the Wire Mills ground on Saturday a game was played between that team and Grappeahall St. Wilfred's. The result was very close and the homesters are to be congratulated on having won, as they did, by six runs. Excellent batting was displayed on both aides. J. Evans made 32, and a score of 31 was credited to Mar- shall. For the visiters Gates made 31 and Ellis 27. Simpson and Watson bowled well for their respective teams, the forrner,taking seven wickets for 36 runs.

On Monday the Wire Mills played Cadishead and Irlens at Cadishead. The homesters batted aid com- piled 73, James Taylor being responsible for 41 runs after an excellent display of batting. The Wire men went in and tied the score for the less of nine wickets. Hawthorn in attempting to make the winning hit was smartly stumped after batting well br 16 runs. Cook also played well for 14, the result being a draw.

An easy win was scored by the Cheshire Lines Engineers over Widnes White Roes on the ground of the latter. The homestors were got out for 21, Duckworth clean bowling 7 wickets for 6 runs. The Engineers compiled 53, of which Barber made 2i and Walker 11.

The second elevens of these clubs played at Warring- ton. In this case the positions were reversed, the vic- tory goilag to the White Rose, who dismissed the Engineers for 11, and repliel wit a a score of 80. Butler batted well for his score of 24, and Vernon and F. Bar- ber made 12 and 10 respectively.

div.head: SWIMMINO.
div.p: SWIMMINO.

The Warrington Club-is to be congratulated on having secured such an important event in the water pole world as the nab v. Midlands match which is to take place at their gala on Saturday evening next, August 19th. This is the most important fixture hold at the local baths since 1894, when the North v. South match took place. Water polo was then, however, in its infancy and great strides have One been made in the game, which is ever increasing in popularity. The Warrington bath is an ideal one for water polo, and is always highly spoken of by the crack players who occasionally visit it. The North team next Saturday will include such well-known exponents of the game as Ripley, said to be the finest player in the world, J. H. Derbyshire, Tom Barrett, of Burslene, who won international hunours as long ago as 1891, R. Sharracks, our local goal-keeper, A. G. Robertson, who it will be remembered kept the English goal intazt in the match with Wales at Newport last year,and other inter- national players. J. A. Jarvis, the amateur swimming champion of the world, will captain the Midlands team. In audition to the polo match an exceptionally good programme is provided. A large entry is expected in the 100 yards handicap, for which many of the leading swimmers have entered. 'the famous Osborne Club hes undertaken to give three very interesting displays, as follows :—Little Tich, aged 11 years, will exhibit his prowess in trick swimming, for which he has already won over 90 pr;zes. J. Wright will perform blindfold and ihigh diving feats; and a trio of champions—in J.H. Derbyshire, 100 yards and 150 yards champion and holder of the 100 yards world's record, P. H. Lister, 1,000 yards champion and second to Janis in the i-mile, 500 yards, and mile, and W H Lister, second in the 100 yards, 150 yards, and 220 yarls championship—will :!give a fast swimming exhibition. It will be seen that the committee while not making too lengthy a programme has provided one which for variety and excellence has not been hitherto equalled in Warringten. Patrons are reminded that ticket holders will be admitted by early doors. The chair will be taken by the president of the club, Coun- cillor Dr. Cannel!.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

Colwyn Bay was the Saturday fixture run for the War- rington Cycling Club, but, owing to the holidays, most of the members went away on their "own." On Tues- day night a party of twenty turned out for a ran to Newton-le-Willows.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

CHURCH BELLRINCIERS' FESTITAL.—On MOIlda? , at Grappenhall, the Chester Diocesan Guild of Church Bell- ringers held their twelftn annual festival. The bell- ringers, numbering about 180, came free* all parts sof Cheshire. The proeeedings opened with a service in the church at eleven o'clock, the sermon being preached by the Lord Bishop of the Diocese. The Bishop and the choir met at the Rectory, and walked te the church. There was a large cougregatioa, among when were the Yen. Archdeacon Barber, master of the Guild, and a number of clergymen. The Bishop took for his text I. Corinthians xiv. 12, " Even so ye, forasmuch as ye are zealous of spiritual gifts, srek that ye may excel to the edifying of the Church," from which he drew lessons of an instructive and interesting character. Special hymns and psalrai were sung.— After the service a general meeting was held in the schools, presided over by the Yen. Archdeacon Barber. The treasurer's statement of accounts was submitted to the meeting, showing a balance in hand of £62 13s for the past year. The report was approved. The election of officers resulted as follows .—Master, the Yen. Arch- deacon Berber ; hon. secretary and treasurer, the Rev R Greenall, rector of Grappentell ; hon. members, the Revs Canon Blencewe (West Kirby), Canon Holme (Great Budwerth), G A Boyd (Macclesfield), H G Mal- lery (Mobberley), G J Howson (Crewe), J H Thorpe (Stockport), and Mr Hatt-Cook (Northwich) ; change ringing members to serve on the general committee. Messrs R T Holding (Crewe), J Dillon (Bebbington), W Walmsley (Macclesfield), F Spence (Grappenhall), J T Bethell (Chester), W Gordon (Stockport), and J Ashmole (Northwi%) ; representatives te serve for three years on the Central Council, Messrs W Gordon (Stockport), and F Spence (Grappenhall). An alteration was made in Guild rule which added an hon. member and a change ringing membor to the general com- mittee. It was decided to hold the next an- neal meeting at Liscard, on August 6th.— Dinner was provided at half-past one in the Large Room. The toast "The Church wad the Queen" having been honoured, the master thanked the Bishop far his kindness in coming, knowing as he did how occupied his lordship's time was, with other matters. He was sure that they would all feel greatly indebted to him tor the excellent advice he had given them that day.— In returning thanks the Bishop said that it gave him great pleasure to come, because lie took a great interest in the asscriation, and he hoped it would continue to flourish.—The dinner over the party broke up to ring at the neiehbouriesz chur'.hes which had been placed at their disposal. Trio followine towers were open for the bell-ringers, during tie afternoon Weight No of bells of tenor. Grappenhall Lyntni Warburton Stretton 6 Daresbury

div.p: FRODSHAM.

BANK HOLIDAT.—SeIdom if ever has Frodsham pre- sented such an appearance as that of Monday last, when the pretty village was crowded to over-flowing with visitors, from all parts of Chshire and Lancashire. Crowds paraded the street 4, and the hill side was beauti- fully sat out with the ever varying costumes Qf the thousands of visitors who cssiyed and accomplished the exhilarating climb. CRICKRT.—A match played at Frodsham, on Wednes- day night, between Frcdsham " A " and Runcorn Shop Assi4tants, resulted in a win for Frodsham by 115 for 5 wickets, t) 106 all out.

SEVERE FIGHTING IN THE HEAVY MOHICAN LOSSES- Disw You', THURSDAY. Despatclri received from the Philippines state that there was a general advance of the American farms from San Fernando at dawn this morning. The troope marched through rain and sunshine alternately until reaching Angeles, about ten miles to the north of San Fernando, and there was fighting mostly all the way, 'The result so far is that the United States troops carried all before them, and lost 10 men killed and 19 wounded. Tie signal for the fight was given by Colonel Bell on the extreme left, who opened fire upon Bonolor, which was captured soon after six o'clock. Then Colonel Powell with the 17th made a demonstratron toward Mexico East, supported by the Third Artillery. There was hot firing for a few minutes, and then the insur- gents started for the north. The armoured train placed in th 3 _American centre steamed out, shelling the rebels' trenches rigut and left. This was followed ny a general advance of all arms, tile country being swept for a distance of five miles by the on-coming United States troops. The difficulties of the ground were great. Toe r Ads were a vriui. The Ninth Infantry charged across a eortafiel J uaaer a 11,1avy fire, the sharp blades of cora cutting the men's hands and faces. They cleared the rebels out ut this position with a loss of three 111S*. Then the Ie was chard ever dinailar ground for a distance of seventeea hundred yards right up to a sugar noose. held by a lard force of the enemy. 'fbere was a stubborn fight, and tau lawae Gould not dislodge the foe, but t e arirtoured train conliog up brought its guns ice play, and the ff.runghold was captured and fifty-four reuels made prisoners.

fhe vict r,uu tc.iops cintinuod t 3 sweep on to the norch,but wee halted after eix miles had been traversed as the otneasy held in force Berne rice and cane fields in- tersected by water. Bell here swung his force down outside tue American outposts,taking the rebels in flank and capturing fifteen prisoners. rum the Americans swept un 'lice more until Angeles was reacked, and a halt was called for the day.

There were SOW) stirring incidents in the fighting- Early in the march an ambulance was cut off and was only rescued by the reserves of the Sixteenth from San Francisco. The Third Battery of Artillery became stuck in a quiekdaud when working round to the north or Bocolor. The gunners were compelled to rescue the piece under heavy fire. The prisoners captured belonged to Agumaldo's own regiment. Gatlings were used and also one Hotc3kisd gum. Taste will Us more fighting to-morrow.
